title: Harnessing gasotransmitters for orthopaedic infection therapy: Mechanisms and advanced delivery platforms
abstract: Orthopaedic infections are increasingly prevalent in the aging population, posing a significant clinical and economic burden. Despite progress in antimicrobial therapies, challenges such as antibiotic resistance and superbug emergence persist. Gas therapy has emerged as a promising strategy for managing orthopaedic infections. Classical gasotransmitters-including nitric oxide (NO), carbon monoxide (CO), and hydrogen sulfide (HS)-exhibit antibacterial and immunomodulatory effects at controlled concentrations, though improper dosing may induce adverse effects. This review critically examines the dual mechanisms through which gasotransmitters combat infection while promoting orthopaedic regeneration. We also survey advanced delivery platforms-such as smart scaffolds, nano-reservoirs, and on-demand release systems-engineered for targeted gasotransmitter delivery to infected bone tissue. Finally, we discuss current limitations and future prospects, aiming to inspire novel biomaterial designs for targeted therapeutic delivery and to advance gas therapy as a viable option for orthopaedic infection treatment.

title: Bioprinted core-shell living material platform for spatially controlled encapsulation of Bacillus subtilis and sustained metabolite exchange
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) represents an escalating global health crisis, demanding alternative strategies to reduce resistant pathogen burden across environments. Microbe-based biocontrol is promising, yet effectively deploying it in practical settings remains challenging. In this study, we present a 3D bioprinted core-shell construct featuring a polyethylene glycol diacrylate (PEGDA) shell with tunable nanoscale porosity, encapsulating germinable spores of the biocontrol agentTH035. This configuration supports long-term spore viability while providing protection from common environmental stressors including UV-C irradiation, ethanol exposure, and desiccation over 4 weeks. The nanoporous PEGDA shell enables effective bacterial confinement while facilitating sufficient metabolite exchange forgermination and growth, as well as suppression of methicillin-resistant(MRSA) growth by approximately one order of magnitude. This approach demonstrates the feasibility of embeddingspores within engineered scaffolds for extended competitive functionality. The versatility and scalability of digital light processing (DLP) based bioprinting offers significant potential for tailored designs and high-throughput manufacturing. This proof-of-concept platform may find future applications in areas such as biomedical packaging, environmental sanitation, and built environment surface coatings, particularly in settings where intermittent moisture or nutrient availability can support spore germination and biocontrol activity.

title: Artificial intelligence catalyzes antimicrobial peptide design
abstract: With broad-spectrum, low resistance, and multifunctional properties, antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are promising therapeutic agents against drug-resistant pathogens, yet their discovery and optimization still remain challenging due to the complexity of sequence-function associations. Artificial intelligence (AI), through the construction of comprehensive data-driven models that assisted with miscellaneous learning strategies, enables de novo peptide design by learning latent representations inherent in peptide sequences as well as their biological properties to ensure physically plausible and biologically relevant predictions. Consequently, this paradigm enhances the likelihood of designing peptide candidates with significantly improved therapeutic potential, reducing resource-intensive trial-and-error processes and revealing the transformative impact of computational innovation in advancing next-generation therapeutics. Here, we provide a snapshot of this field and survey two modes of AI-driven technologies for AMP design, one concentrated on identifying whether current data possess antimicrobial activity (identification-oriented) and the other on generating AMP candidates with potential therapeutic properties (generation-oriented). We also highlight the challenges and limitations that still hinder AMP development even accelerated by AI, as well as the foreseeable prospects, from finer-grained explorations to model-driven data enrichment and model enhancement.

title: Antifungal mechanisms of volatile organic compounds and lactic acid produced by Lactiplantibacillus pentosus and their biocontrol application in fresh corn against Fusarium graminearum
abstract: Fusarium graminearum causes cereal spoilage and mycotoxin production. Currently, biocontrol microorganisms have emerged as a safe and promising strategy to manage the contamination of toxin-producing fungi in cereal grains. The primary objective was to elucidate the antifungal mechanism of an isolated strain of Lactiplantibacillus pentosus Q11 against F. graminearum and to evaluate the preservative effects of its cell-free supernatant (CFS) in fresh sweet corn. In vitro antifungal assays of L. pentosus Q11 showed strong antagonistic activity against F. graminearum, Aspergillus flavus, and Penicillium expansum, as well as the ability to reduce zearalenone. Moreover, whole-genome analysis revealed no genes related to virulence and antimicrobial resistance, and no hemolytic activity was observed, which suggested the potential safety of strain Q11. Moreover, the CFS of L. pentosus Q11 effectively inhibited the mycelial growth of F. graminearum, disrupted hyphal integrity, and induced fungal cell death. Moreover, 3 organic acids and 38 volatile compounds in the CFS of Q11 strain were identified by SPME-GC-MS and HPLC, in which 2-nonanone, 2-methylpyrazine, lactic acid, acetic acid were predominant compounds. The CFS and lactic acid combined with 2-nonanone severely damaged hyphae of F. graminearum, by disrupting cell membrane and wall, leading to leakage of intracellular substances, showing a synergistic antifungal effect of the two vital compounds. Subsequently, the treatments of CFS and combined agents significantly decreased 88.05% - 89.52% of fungal populations, and AFBand DON mycotoxin accumulation in fresh sweet corn after 12 days of storage compared to the control. The malondialdehyde content in the treated corn was decreased by 29.25% - 31.50%, consistent with the higher activities of POD and APX, thereby preserving their sensory attributes and nutritional quality. Metabolomic analysis revealed that L-glutamate, γ-glutamylcysteine, and oxidized glutathione were significantly downregulated in the glutathione metabolism pathway in the treated corn, indicating that CFS containing lactic acid and 2-nonanone could repress fungal growth and alleviate oxidative stress in fresh sweet corn. Overall, these findings demonstrate that L. pentosus Q11 with synergistic volatile organic compounds and lactic acid is a promising biocontrol agent in preserving fresh sweet corn.

title: Therapeutic effects and mechanisms of neutrophil membrane-coated MXene (Ti (3) C (2) T (x) ) nanoparticles for sepsis treatment
abstract: Sepsis, a life-threatening organ dysfunction from a dysregulated infection response, remains a high-mortality global health burden characterized by the systemic overproduction of pro-inflammatory mediators and reactive oxygen and nitrogen species. Timely anti-infective/anti-inflammatory interventions in the early onset window drastically improve sepsis prognosis, yet current therapeutic efficacy remains severely constrained by the global antibiotic resistance crisis. As a two-dimensional nanomaterial, TiCTMXene displays potent intrinsic antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory activities. We herein engineer a neutrophil membrane-coated TiCTnanoplatform (NM@TiCTNPs) for targeted sepsis therapy. Experimental validation confirms this formulation mitigates sepsis-triggered oxidative stress injury via synergistic antioxidant pathways, with favorable colloidal stability and confirmed in vitro biocompatibility. In CLP-induced murine sepsis models, it attenuates systemic pro-inflammatory cascades, alleviates hypothermia and multi-organ damage, and improves survival. Collectively, this multifunctional platform integrating targeted antibacterial action and oxidative stress modulation presents a promising candidate for sepsis translational therapy.

title: Rational design of inhaled antibacterials targeting alveolar macrophages for efficient killing of resistant bacteria associated with lower respiratory tract infections (LRTIs)
abstract: Lower respiratory tract infections (LRTIs), caused by antibiotic-resistant bacteria, are a leading cause of global death and morbidity. One of the principal limitations in treating respiratory bacterial infections is inefficient delivery and appropriate therapeutic drug concentrations to infected cells, as required to kill resistant bacteria. Inhaled antibiotic delivery technology specifically delivers antibacterials directly into the infected cells of the lungs and provides the required therapeutic concentration at a very low delivered dose, with a greatly reduced risk of systemic adverse effects. An alveolar macrophage (AM)-targeted antibiotic delivery strategy utilizing receptor-ligand interactions or stimuli-responsive mechanisms of drug release demonstrated efficient killing of intracellular bacteria. The rational design of antibacterials or formulations for inhalation is the key to achieving this goal. Based on ligand chemistry, decorating antibiotic carriers with ligands that target specific AM receptors is a novel strategy to ensure precise antibiotic delivery to the site of infection while reducing both the side effects associated with high systemic doses and the risk of further promoting antibiotic resistance. This review highlights advances in AM-targeted inhaled antibacterials, identification of appropriate ligands for specific AM receptors, mechanisms of interaction, and subsequent release of antibiotics through carrier degradation, pH-responsive behavior, or enzymatic cleavage to eradicate resistant bacteria. Finally, we discuss the ongoing challenges and future directions for AM-targeted inhaled antibacterials against LRTIs.

title: Rifamycin use and gut microbial antibiotic resistance genes in cirrhosis: Results from a double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trial
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance gene (ARG) carriage is associated with poor outcomes in patients with liver cirrhosis, which is worsened by repeated antibiotic exposure and hospitalizations. While the semi-synthetic rifamycin derivative, rifaximin, has recently been linked to ARG expansion preclinically, the effects of rifamycin SV MMX (RiVM) on the gut resistome remain unknown. We evaluated longitudinal resistome changes with RiVM in cirrhosis. The randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled RIVET trial (15 RiVM, 15 placebo) included compensated cirrhosis patients who underwent shotgun metagenomic sequencing before/after 30 days of therapy. ARGs were annotated using the Comprehensive Antibiotic Resistance Database. The longitudinal resistome was evaluated using univariable and multi-variable methods (LEfSe, paired-Wilcoxon testing, and MaAsLin3), and machine learning (ML) was used to determine ARG changes at subject and group levels. RiVM induced minimal perturbation of the gut resistome, without significant change in ARGs versus after FDR adjustment. Complementary approaches (univariable and multivariable) identified a trend towards lower vancomycin resistance ARGs, including vanW and vanT operon-associated genes, after RiVM exposure. In contrast, several Enterobacteriaceae-associated multidrug efflux regulators (including evgS, emrK, and mdtA) showed nominal increases post-rifamycin that did not withstand FDR. Group-level ML demonstrated limited discrimination between groups; however, within-subject longitudinal models achieved improved classification performance. No increase in infections or treatment-related safety concerns was observed. We conclude that rifamycin MMX was not associated with infections and did not enrich antimicrobial resistance genes compared to placebo in a small randomized 30-day clinical trial in patients with compensated cirrhosis. There was a tendency towards reduced vancomycin resistance and ARG reduction after rifamycin exposure.NCT04082780 www.clinicaltrials.gov.

title: Integrated multi-omics analysis reveals distinct metabolic signatures and gut microbiome alterations across the pediatric obesity spectrum
abstract: Pediatric obesity drives extensive metabolic remodeling across gut and systemic compartments, yet integrated multi-omics characterization across the full obesity spectrum remains incomplete. We studied 57 Mexican children stratified by BMI into normal weight (NW, = 15), overweight (Ow, = 8), and obese (Ob, = 34) groups using liver enzyme profiling, untargeted fecal and serum metabolomics, 16S rRNA gut microbiome sequencing, and antimicrobial resistance assessment. Demographic parameters were comparable across groups ( = 0.632), minimizing confounding. Gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT) showed the strongest obesity association (25.5 ± 6.0 vs. 15.0 ± 3.0 U/L in NW; < 0.001), outperforming ALT and AST as an early hepatic stress biomarker. Metabolomic profiling identified 1088 altered fecal and 1041 altered serum metabolites (Ob vs. NW), with enriched pathways spanning aromatic amino acid metabolism, one-carbon metabolism, glycolysis/TCA cycle, and nucleotide biosynthesis. Key perturbations included upregulation of kynurenine and 3-nitrotyrosine alongside downregulation of bile acids and purine metabolites. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed 78, 95, and 28 differentially abundant taxa in Ow vs. NW, Ob vs. Ow, and Ob vs. NW comparisons, with elevated beta-diversity dispersion in obesity. Co-abundance network analysis uncovered disrupted metabolite-metabolite and taxon‒taxon interactions, including loss of beneficial SCFA-producing consortia, bile acid dysregulation, and altered amino acid-microbiome coupling. Integration of microbiome and metabolome data revealed high-magnitude genus-metabolite correlations-including Lachnospiraceae with acetate ( = 0.92) and Tyzzerella with vulpecholate ( = 0.94)-mapping to mechanistic pathways linking SCFAs, bile acids, tryptophan-indole derivatives, and aromatic amino acids to obesity pathogenesis. These findings identify GGT as a sensitive pediatric metabolic biomarker and provide mechanistic insights and therapeutic targets for early intervention.

Use of a molecular syndromic panel for the etiological diagnosis of bloodstream infections in critically ill patients: impact on clinical outcomes and antimicrobial use from a multicenter, prospective study
abstract: Bloodstream infections (BSI) frequently occur in critically ill patients and remain associated with high mortality rates. A prospective, observational, multicenter investigation was carried out through the MULTI-SITA platform to evaluate how the addition of a molecular syndromic panel, the BIOFIREBlood Culture Identification 2 (BCID2) Panel (BCID2 panel), to conventional blood culture diagnostics influenced key clinical endpoints and antimicrobial use. The primary endpoint was all-cause mortality within 30 days following the onset of BSI. Among the 126 included critically ill patients with BSI, multivariable analysis identified SOFA score (hazard ratio [HR] 1.21, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.09-1.34, < 0.001), other concomitant infections requiring antibiotic therapy (HR 2.61, 95% CI 1.18-5.79, = 0.018), and BSI caused byspp. (HR 4.35, 95% CI 1.10-17.18, = 0.036),(HR 3.38, 95% CI 1.26-9.08, = 0.016), or(HR 15.97, 95% CI 2.43-104.54, = 0.004) as associated with increased mortality, while no association was observed between use of the BCID2 panel and mortality (HR 0.97, 95% CI 0.42-2.25, = 0.941). In secondary analyses, the use of the BCID2 panel resulted in more events of either early antimicrobial de-escalation or initiation of appropriate therapy at day one from BSI onset compared with a standard blood culture workflow (55.6% vs. 31.7%, = 0.015). In critically ill patients with BSI, implementation of a molecular syndromic panel influenced antimicrobial management decisions without affecting mortality. Additional investigations are warranted to clarify the long-term antimicrobial stewardship implications of treatment strategies guided by molecular syndromic panels-based diagnostic workflows.

title: Responsible use of new antibiotics for critically ill patients suffering from infections due to carbapenem-resistant organisms-a narrative review for an enablement strategy
abstract: Infections caused by multidrug-resistant Gram-negative (MDR-GN) bacteria, particularly carbapenem-resistant organisms (CROs), constitute a significant burden in critically ill patients (CIPs). A multidisciplinary, collaborative approach is essential for responsible antibiotic use in CIPs, balancing the necessity for effective treatment with mitigation of antimicrobial resistance (AMR). While the efficacy of existing antibiotics against CROs is increasingly limited due to resistance development and suboptimal pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic properties, several barriers impede the widespread adoption of new agents, including selective susceptibility testing, limited availability, high costs, and concerns regarding the fostering of resistance. Antimicrobial stewardship (AMS) strategies aim to optimize antibiotic use; however, there is an ongoing debate between restrictive and enabling approaches for new antibiotics in CIPs with CRO infections. While restrictive strategies focus on limiting antibiotic use to mitigate resistance, they may delay necessary treatment and negatively impact professional culture. Enablement strategies promote informed decision-making and accessibility when needed but require substantial workforce and expertise. In this narrative review and expert opinion, we propose an algorithm supporting a coordinated AMS approach in CIPs, emphasizing the importance of early diagnosis and appropriate therapy. We advocate for an enablement strategy for new antibiotics in CIPs with MDR-GN infections, aiming to reduce mortality and toxicity associated with older agents. This strategy should be integrated into local AMS programmes under the guidance of experienced clinicians.

title: Modelling the transmission and burden of ESBL-producing Enterobacterales from a One Health perspective in Singapore
abstract: The long-term burden of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in hyper-urbanised settings, shaped by complex, multi-sectoral transmission dynamics across human, animal, and environmental reservoirs, remains poorly understood. Using Singapore as a case study, we applied a dynamic One Health modelling framework to explore how ESBL-producing Enterobacterales infections and deaths may evolve over the next decade and identify critical control pathways. We developed a deterministic, compartmental One Health transmission model, the first to integrate hospital, community, companion animal, and environmental reservoirs, calibrated to ten years of national hospital surveillance data (2012-2021) using Markov Chain Monte Carlo Bayesian methods. We projected the baseline disease burden over a 10-year reporting horizon and compared it with counterfactual scenarios while employing global and local sensitivity analyses to identify influential parameters. Over this period, the model projected a total burden of 208,179 clinical ESBL-producing Enterobacterales infections (95% uncertainty interval [UI] 121,669-307,053) and 5567 (95% UI 3660-7806) deaths, with 3491 deaths specifically attributable to ESBL-producing Enterobacterales. Community decolonization strongly influenced infection burdens in both community and hospital settings; a 100% reduction in this process was projected to add nearly 1.8 million additional infections and more than 45,000 resistant-infection deaths across hospital and community settings in Singapore over 10 years. Our dynamic One Health model quantifies these inter-sectoral transmission pathways and identifies clear intervention priorities. While preventing progression from colonisation to infection is vital for reducing hospital-specific mortality, comprehensive system-wide control may benefit from targeting the community reservoir. Ultimately, the modelling framework developed here provides a robust, transferable tool for other global cities to design and evaluate integrated One Health AMR control strategies to mitigate urgent public health threats and associated socio-economic consequences for urban populations and global healthcare systems.

title: Co-occurrence of antimicrobial resistance and reduced disinfectant susceptibility in Campylobacter spp. along the chicken supply chain: A farm-to-fork public health concern
abstract: spp. are major foodborne pathogens, yet integrated farm-to-fork studies addressing contamination dynamics, antimicrobial resistance, disinfectant susceptibility, lineage dissemination, and genome structure remain limited. In this study, a batch of yellow-feathered broilers in China was tracked from farm to slaughterhouse and retail to investigatealong the chicken supply chain. Integrated phenotype-genotype analysis showed clear associations between major resistance phenotypes and determinants, including T86I,(O),(B), 23S2075 A > G, andOXA-61. Multilocus sequence typing (MLST) identified ST829 as a dissemination-associated high-risk lineage persisting from farm to retail. By integrating farm-to-fork surveillance with resistance and genomic analyses, this study highlights the food safety significance of poultry-associatedand provides a valuable basis for risk-oriented monitoring and targeted intervention in the chicken supply chain.

abstract: spp. are emerging foodborne pathogens posing public health risks through zoonotic transmission in agricultural settings. Characterizing their phylogenetic relatedness, antimicrobial resistance (AMR), and virulence factors is critical for assessing their impact on food safety and health in Ghana and Tanzania. We collected 144isolates (139 from farm animals and 5 from human clinical cases) and analyzed their genomes using molecular phylogenetics, antimicrobial resistance gene (ARG) profiling, and virulence gene identification. Phylogenetic analysis confirmedas the predominant species with two distinct subclades exhibiting multiple drug resistance. Notably, we identified a second clade ofthat may represent a novel species. Additionally, a potential new subspecies withinwas detected, supported by genomic and digital DNA:DNA hybridization (dDDH) analyses. A multiple antibiotic-resistantisolate was found to harbor a resistance plasmid encoding five AMR genes. The pangenome reflected an open genome structure with a vast accessory gene pool related to resistance and virulence. ARGs conferring tetracycline, macrolide, and aminoglycoside resistance were widespread, with commercial farm isolates showing higher resistance burdens than those from smallholder farms. Virulence genes varied, illustrating broad genetic diversity and adaptive potential. This study highlights genomic plasticity and emerging resistance inspp. from human and animal sources in sub-Saharan Africa. The discovery of new clades and a resistant plasmid underscore the need for enhanced One Health surveillance to control the spread and impact of these pathogens on public health and food safety.

Extended spectrum beta lactamases and carbapenemase-producing Escherichia coli in humans, animals and the environment in East Africa: a scoping review
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is escalating in East Africa through close human-animal-environment interactions. Extended-spectrum beta-lactamases (ESBL) and carbapenemase-producingare clinically critical pathogens, yet local evidence is limited. This scoping review synthesizes evidence on ESBL and carbapenemase-producingin East Africa to inform One Health AMR control strategies. Following PRISMA-ScR guidelines, PubMed and Scopus were searched, identifying 279 records published between 2015 and 2025. After removing duplicates and screening, 185 articles were assessed for eligibility; 154 studies spanning human, animal and environmental sources met the inclusion criteria. Two reviewers independently extracted epidemiological, microbiological and molecular data in Covidence, including resistance genes and transmission evidence. The 154 included studies spanned 11 East African countries, led by Ethiopia ( = 55), Tanzania ( = 39) and Uganda ( = 22). Most studies (85.7%) were cross-sectional and human-focused (68.2%), with only 19 (12.3%) using a multi-sector One Health design. Overall, 21,554isolates were recovered from 74,700 samples. ESBL prevalence was reported in 117 studies (76.0%, median 46.8%) and carbapenemase prevalence in 65 (42.2%, median 3.3%), representing heterogeneous study-level estimates.predominated (89.9%), led by(26.1%); reported carbapenemase genes included,,andWhole-genome sequencing in 30 studies (19.5%) identified high-risk clones ST131, ST10, ST38 and ST410, though animal, food-chain and environmental sectors remained underrepresented. This review maps the current evidence on landscape for ESBL/carbapenemase- producingin East Africa, highlighting gaps in surveillance that are largely due to heterogeneity of available genomics data and limited longitudinal data within the "One Health" sectors. We recommend scaling up genomic capacity and standardized longitudinal surveillance to better understand national and regional AMR transmission and MDRinfections.

title: Dietary licorice improves carcass yield, hepatocellular protection, gut health, oxidative status, and cecal bacterial balance in broiler chickens
abstract: Over the past decade, phytotherapy such as licorice has attracted research as an alternative to antibiotic growth promoters in broiler production, driven by rising concerns over antimicrobial resistance. However, the consistency of its effects across productive, physiological, and health outcomes remains inconsistent. This meta-analysis quantitatively synthesized published experimental evidence on the effects of dietary licorice on growth performance, carcass yield, blood indices, visceral organs, oxidative status, intestinal morphology, and cecal bacterial balance in broiler chickens. A systematic literature search identified studies published between 2010 and 2025, and effect sizes were computed (Hedges'; 95% confidence interval). Pooled estimates were derived under the random-effects model using the restricted maximum likelihood estimator, with between-study heterogeneity characterized bythe-statistic. Univariable mixed-effects meta-regression was conducted to identify study-level moderators of treatment response, and publication bias was assessed using a funnel plot and the Rosenberg fail-safe N criterion. Dietary licorice did not affect feed intake or the feed conversion ratio, but it did increase body weight gain (BWG; SMD = 0.289; = 0.002), breast, thigh, gizzard, and bursa weights ( < 0.05). Gut integrity also improved with the villus height/crypt depth ratio (SMD = 0.931; = 0.041), andspp. counts (SMD = 0.266; = 0.003) increased, whilepopulations were suppressed (SMD = -1.737; < 0.001). Overall, the findings support that licorice enhances body weight gain, with route, duration, sex, and strain moderating efficacy.

abstract: ()is a globally pervasive and economically significant pathogen in bovine intramammary infections (IMIs) and is responsible for both clinical and subclinical mastitis. This study systematically investigated the global epidemiology offrom bovine IMIs, addressing antimicrobial resistance (AMR) amongthrough a meta-analysis. A total of 143 studies published between 2000 and 2025 were identified through comprehensive searches, which were based on predefined inclusion criteria. The data were systematically extracted, and the statistical analyses were performed in R (v4.5.2). The meta-analysis included 143 studies (145,457 samples), with a pooledprevalence of 24.78% and high heterogeneity (I = 99.51%). Subgroup analyses demonstrated significant heterogeneity in prevalence by study design, publication year, and region, with greater heterogeneity in cross-sectional studies (I>95%, < 0.001). Meta-regression identified sample size as a significant source of heterogeneity (β = -0.00002, = 0.02; R = 3.41%). The highest prevalence was reported in Cameroon (67%), Sri Lanka (64.3%), Indonesia (57%), and India (44%), with the lowest prevalence reported in Poland (0.7%), Taiwan (2.0%), Australia (5.5%), and New Zealand (5.3%). AMR was highest for doxycycline (70.7%), penicillin (65.2%), and ampicillin (62.8%); moderate to oxacillin (44.6%) and vancomycin (40.2%); and lowest for gentamicin (27.5%) and amikacin (18.3%). is highly prevalent in bovine IMIs worldwide, with marked regional heterogeneity and substantial resistance to commonly used antimicrobials, emphasizing the urgent need for targeted surveillance, prudent antimicrobial use, and improved mastitis control strategies at the global and regional levels.

N-acetylcysteine as an adjunct to antibiotics against bacterial biofilms: A systematic review of in vitro evidence
abstract: N-acetylcysteine (NAC) is investigated as an antibiotic adjunct, but acidity, formulation and experimental context complicate interpretation. We evaluated comparative in-vitro evidence while distinguishing biofilm prevention, established-biofilm treatment and resistance evolution. MEDLINE/PubMed, Embase, Scopus and Web of Science were searched through August 2026, with supplementary searching. Extraction distinguished NAC preparation and exposure pH, medium, hydrodynamics, NAC-alone controls, treatment intent and interaction methodology. Results were synthesized by experimental context, regimen, phase and endpoint without pooling or whole-study efficacy voting. Fifty-five studies were included: 7 evaluated combination exposure during formation only, 37 after establishment only, 9 both, and 2 resistance evolution. NAC-alone arms were documented in 39 studies, partial or formulation-specific in 9, and not identified in 7. Only two studies included a continuous-flow model. Selected combinations improved biofilm-associated outcomes, but intrinsic-acidic and neutralized preparations, biomass and viability endpoints, and planktonic versus biofilm interaction tests were not interchangeable. Liposomal and catheter-lock findings differed by dose matching, isolate and control set. Polymyxin findings varied with organism, resistance background, medium and exposure; rifampicin-alone and rifampicin-containing multidrug comparators addressed different questions. NAC is a context-dependent experimental adjunct, not an established class-wide antibiotic potentiator. The evidence does not support clinical antibiotic dose reduction or routine NAC combination therapy. Translation requires controlled final exposure pH, matched monotherapy and formulation controls, clinically relevant background regimens, viable-burden and regrowth outcomes, and resistance monitoring.

Combating antimicrobial resistance through multimodal data via artificial intelligence
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) poses a critical global health challenge, leading to substantial mortality and economic losses without science-based interventions. Conventional approaches to combating AMR have important limitations in addressing this escalating threat. Recent advances in AI, including deep learning, large language models, and protein language models, provide new opportunities to integrate multimodal data for AMR research. However, evidence remains uneven, with many approaches limited to computational benchmarking rather than real-world validation. Here, we critically review AI applications in AMR, focusing on rapid diagnosis, therapeutic discovery, and clinical decision support. AI-based diagnostic models can identify resistant pathogens and predict resistance profiles, but most lack prospective clinical evaluation. AI-assisted drug discovery and alternative therapies have generated promising candidates, although most remain at computational, in vitro, or early preclinical stages. Large language models may support decision-making, but their clinical use remains preliminary. Successful translation of AI into clinical and One Health practice will require representative datasets, independent validation, prospective evaluation, and robust governance.

abstract: Mastitis is a multifactorial disease with major consequences for production, animal welfare, and public health, yet it remains less studied in goats than in cows. Moreover, reports of antimicrobial resistance among bacteria isolated from mastitic goats are scarce. In Ethiopia, treatment decisions for mastitis largely rely on empirical clinical experience rather than routine antimicrobial susceptibility testing. To address this gap, a cross-sectional study was conducted from November to December 2024 in Waghimra, Amhara, Ethiopia, to identify the major bacterial causes of mastitis and to evaluate their antimicrobial susceptibility patterns. Bacterial isolation, identification, and antimicrobial susceptibility testing followed standard protocols, and statistical analyses were performed using Stata 17 and WHONET software. The overall goat-level mastitis prevalence was 24.69% (98/397), comprising 2.52% (10/397) clinical and 22.28% (88/395) subclinical mastitis.spp. (47/129; 36.43%) was the predominant isolate, followed by(12/129; 9.30%) andspp. (3/129; 2.33%). Allisolates were resistant to ampicillin (37/37; 100%) and showed considerable resistance to tetracycline (16/37; 43.24%), but remained highly susceptible to kanamycin (36/37; 97.30%), chloramphenicol, and gentamicin (35/37; 94.59% each).andspp. were highly susceptible to most antimicrobials tested, except ampicillin. Multidrug resistance was detected in 13.46% (7 out of 52) of isolates, occurring exclusively amongspp. Subclinical mastitis, mainly caused byspp., was highly prevalent in the study area, showing complete ampicillin resistance and considerable tetracycline resistance. These findings have important implications for milk production, animal welfare, and public health, given local raw milk consumption.

Strengthening One Health Antimicrobial Resistance Surveillance in Bangladesh: Insights from the Fleming fund country grant
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is an escalating global public health concern, with particularly severe implications for low and middle-income countries such as Bangladesh. In Bangladesh context, fragmented surveillance systems and the extensive use of antimicrobials across human, animal, and aquaculture sectors contribute to the rapid emergence and spread of resistance. Strengthening integrated surveillance through a One Health approach is therefore crucial to support effective policy development and response strategies. This review outlines the policy, implementation, and key outcomes of the Fleming Fund Country Grant in Bangladesh between 2020 and 2025. It draws upon multiple data sources, including programme reports, routine AMR surveillance data, laboratory capacity-building initiatives, and stakeholder engagement activities across human, animal, aquaculture, and environmental sectors. Through this initiative, a coordinated national AMR surveillance network was established, comprising 20 laboratories across multiple sectors, including three designated national reference laboratories. The initiative strengthened surveillance through the introduction of standardized protocols and SOPs, improved diagnostic capacity, skilled workforce, and implementation of laboratory quality assurance systems, including EQA and NEQA. These measures enhanced the accuracy, consistency, and reliability of AMR surveillance data. In addition, the establishment of a national AMR data integration platform facilitated real time data sharing and evidence-based decision-making. A total of 208,346 bacterial isolates were analyzed, with AST results reported to the AMR dashboard across the human, and animal, health sectors. Overall, the Fleming Fund programme has made a substantial contribution to strengthening integrated AMR surveillance in Bangladesh by operationalizing a One Health framework. Continued political commitment, increased domestic investment, and the institutionalization of surveillance systems will be essential to sustain these gains and ensure long-term resilience against AMR.

Microfluidic-assembled curcumin ionizable lipid nanoparticles enhance aqueous delivery and antibiofilm activity against Staphylococcus aureus
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance and biofilm-associated infections demand novel therapeutic strategies. Curcumin is a natural polyphenol with broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity; however, its clinical utility is fundamentally constrained by negligible aqueous solubility and limited biofilm penetration. Here, we used microfluidic assembly to prepare curcumin-loaded ionizable lipid nanoparticles (Cur@LNP) with three clinically established ionizable lipids (SM-102, MC-3, and ALC-0315). The resulting formulations were uniform, with hydrodynamic diameters of approximately 90 nm and polydispersity indices near 0.1. Relative to free curcumin in DMSO, Cur@LNP lowered the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) 8-fold and the minimum bactericidal concentration (MBC) 16-fold against planktonic, and markedly reduced viable biofilm-resident cells at matched concentrations. Scanning electron microscopy showed that Cur@LNP treatment remodeled mature biofilms into irregular, debris-rich aggregates with reduced extracellular matrix coverage. Notably, antimicrobial performance was indistinguishable across the three structurally distinct ionizable lipids at every concentration tested. Within this in vitro, single-strain system, the antibiofilm effect is therefore dominated by the cargo (curcumin) rather than by ionizable-lipid chemistry, and it is most likely attributed to enhanced aqueous solubilization of curcumin rather than to engagement of the lipid headgroup with the biofilm matrix. These results position microfluidic-assembled ionizable LNPs as a reproducible, scalable solubilization platform for poorly water-soluble natural antimicrobials.

title: Metagenomic analysis of commensal small mammal samples from an international cargo shipping area, Bangkok Port, reveals potential zoonotic pathogens and implications for One Health surveillance
abstract: Commensal small mammals, such as rats and shrews, are recognized reservoirs for numerous zoonotic pathogens; however, their role in pathogen circulation at transport hubs remains underexplored. This study employs shotgun metagenomic sequencing to characterize microbial communities and assess zoonotic potential in tissue samples from commensal small mammals captured at Bangkok Port, an international cargo shipping hub in Thailand between June and August 2025. Following host read depletion, taxonomic profiling was performed to identify bacterial taxa of public health relevance, including sequences assigned tospp.,,, and. The virulence factor and antibiotic resistance gene profiles revealed that some of these pathogens have pathogenic potential and are related to drug-resistant bacteria. In addition,was identified as a shared taxon among rats, shrews, and their associated fleas. The findings support the ecological roles of mammalian hosts and their ectoparasites as reservoirs for pathogens of public health concern. These results emphasize the need to strengthen surveillance programs for commensal small mammals to monitor and mitigate the spread of transboundary pathogens at international maritime gateways.

Wild boar as a sentinel species for ecosystem health surveillance: A review
abstract: Sentinel surveillance uses selected species that are widely distributed, easily sampled, and exposed to multiple health threats as indicators of ecosystem health. The Eurasian wild boar () is a broadly distributed game species that meets these conditions. We conducted a systematic review to assess the suitability of the wild boar as a sentinel or indicator species for monitoring health hazards relevant to ecosystem health, focusing on the hazards monitored, methods, justification for use, perceived performance, limitations, and proposed improvements. We identified 86 studies explicitly framing the wild boar as a sentinel species, covering a wide range of hazards, including 30 pathogens, 44 environmental contaminants, two biological toxins and 13 antimicrobial resistance (AMR) indicators. It was used to monitor pathogens (57%), environmental contaminants (31.4%), AMR (12.8%), and biological toxins (3.5%). Research effort was concentrated in Europe (84.9%) and relied mostly on hunted animals (90.7%). Wild boar were frequently selected as sentinels due to their previous use as indicators of ecosystem health in the literature, omnivorous diet, wide distribution, and accessibility as game species. However, hunting-based sampling may introduce biases, while post-mortem conditions and ecological variability may affect results. Despite this, 74.4% of studies supported their use as sentinels, particularly for pathogens and environmental contaminants. In contrast, their perceived suitability for AMR was more variable, and no quality assessment was available for biological toxins. Overall, wild boar sentinel surveillance is considered logistically efficient and valuable for monitoring ecosystem health hazards. However, its effectiveness is context-dependent and influenced by methodological and ecological limitations. Improving surveillance design through systematic sampling, alternative sample sources (e.g., found-dead animals or non-invasive methods), integration of multi-species data, and inclusion of covariates could enhance the reliability of findings within a One Health framework.

title: Global spread of carbapenem-resistant Providencia driven by high-risk lineages and plasmid co-evolution
abstract: Carbapenem-resistant(CRP) is a formidable opportunistic pathogen with extensive drug resistance, posing an increasing threat to human, animal, and environmental health. However, its global genomic epidemiology and resistome-plasmidome co-evolution within a One Health context remain poorly understood. Here, we conducted a comprehensive population genomic and plasmid analysis of 1197 CRP isolates from 35 countries spanning 2012-2025. We reclassified the CRP population into ninespecies, identifyingandas established epidemic species alongside the rapid emergence ofand. We pinpointed 2019 as a critical inflection point, marking the transition from endemic stability to rapid global epidemic expansion (80.8% isolates in 2019-2025). Ten intercontinentally disseminated high-risk sequence types (e.g., ST46, ST79), each with strict species-ST specificity, were responsible for global spread. Thegene (62.4% prevalence) was the predominant carbapenem gene, exhibiting strong geographic and species specificity and mutual exclusion with other major carbapenem genes. Plasmids encoded approximately 80% of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) genes, with 78.0% of these plasmids belonging to 75 stable clusters. These clusters evolved a dual specialist-generalist strategy, with the broad-host-range cluster 72 mediating interspecies AMR transmission and cluster 7 acting as a super-vector carrying six carbapenem genes. Importantly, CRP circulated across interconnected human, animal, and environmental reservoirs, with distinct host-associated species distributions suggesting ecological niche adaptation and potential cross-host dissemination of resistance determinants. These findings demonstrate that the global expansion of CRP is driven by the combined evolution of high-risk clones and mobile genetic elements across interconnected ecological sectors, underscoring the need for integrated One Health surveillance and coordinated interventions spanning clinical, veterinary, agricultural, and environmental settings.

Five years of wastewater surveillance reveal COVID-19-Associated amplification and seasonal shifts in bla (KPC) and bla (NDM)
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) has intensified in recent years, raising concerns about the potential impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on AMR dynamics. However, the influence of pandemic on the enviromental occurrence and dissemination of antibiotic-resistant genes (ARGs) remains under investigation. Wastewater-based epidemiology (WBE) provides an integrated view of community-level AMR dynamics, yet long-term assessments spanning the pandemic period remain limited. This study investigated the occurrence, temporal patterns, and seasonal behavior of two clinically relevant carbapenemase genes,and, in raw wastewater from the Attica region over a five-year period (July 2021-September 2025). A sensitive and specific 3-plex qPCR assay was developed and analytically validated for the simultaneous quantification of,, and 16S rRNA, the latter serving as a stable bacterial load indicator. Across the monitoring period,was consistently detected, showing a steady increase and reaching its highest concentrations in 2023, whileexhibited intermittent but pronounced surges, particularly in 2023. Comparison with community SARS-CoV-2 viral loads suggest temporal association with AMR signatures in wastewater. Seasonal analysis showed non-uniform patterns, with atypical warm-season peaks of both ARGs in 2023-2024 and a return to classical autumn-winter peaks in 2025, suggesting a gradual restoration of pre-pandemic seasonality. To our knowledge, this is among the first long-term WBE studies to characterize post-COVID-19 shifts in ARG occurrence and seasonality. The results demonstrate that the pandemic period was associated with elevated and fluctuating ARG levels in the urban wastewater system, emphasizing the need for sustained AMR monitoring. These findings address critical knowledge gaps in environmental AMR surveillance and support the integration of WBE into public health strategies aimed at mitigating AMR dissemination.

Genomic epidemiology to investigate the origins and zoonotic implications of antibiotic-resistant Escherichia coli on beef and lamb meat sold by independent butchers in Wales
abstract: Many studies have identified antibiotic resistant (ABR)on meat. Appropriate hand hygiene and cooking practices should minimize the risk of gastrointestinal colonisation with ABRfound on meat, and the subsequent chance of causing resistant opportunistic extraintestinal infection. There are large gaps in our understanding of the prevalence, origins and zoonotic potential of ABRfound on meat, however, and particularly for meat reared in extensive farming systems. Wales is a devolved nation within the United Kingdom having large populations of extensively-reared sheep and beef cattle. To help address knowledge gaps around ABRon extensively reared meat, therefore, beef mince and lamb loin/leg steaks/chops were purchased from 50 (beef) and 46 (lamb) independent butchers across Wales. Following enrichment culture, 200 g meat samples were found to be positive forresistant to amoxicillin (31% positivity), streptomycin (28%), spectinomycin (29%), amoxicillin-clavulanate (11%), 3rd generation cephalosporins (2%) and fluoroquinolones (5%). Phylogenetic analysis confirmed that Welsh lamb meat ABRisolates ( = 78) are more closely related to those found in faecal samples collected around sheep ( = 352) than around beef cattle ( = 361) on Welsh farms. This suggests that faecal contamination at or around slaughter is their primary origin. We found no closely related meat/infection clones (<20 SNPs distant and the same antibiotic resistance genes) when comparing ABRfrom Welsh meat ( = 91) and those causing extraintestinal infections in people ( = 2387) in an English region bordering Wales. We conclude, therefore, that the wider zoonotic implications of finding ABRon beef and lamb meat sold at independent butchers in Wales are small, though a more geographically and temporarily contemporaneous survey is warranted to address this further.

Sewage surveillance for assessing clinical antibiotic resistance prevalence: Combining metagenomic and phenotypic data
abstract: Surveillance of antibiotic resistance in clinical isolates is a cornerstone for the management of bacterial infections but is limited in large parts of the world, often due to lack of resources. Sewage surveillance has been proposed as a promising, resource-efficient complement to the traditional surveillance approach based on samples from many individual patients. Both phenotypic data on resistance in sewage isolates and abundance of antibiotic resistance genes in sewage have been shown to correlate with resistance prevalence in clinical isolates. Here, we aimed to directly compare and combine an isolate-based and a gene-based sewage surveillance approach to evaluate what best can reflect clinical resistance rates. The two approaches, based on susceptibility testing of collectedisolates and metagenomic sequencing, respectively, were applied to municipal sewage samples collected in ten European countries. The data generated was related to available data on resistance to aminopenicillins, fluoroquinolones, third generation cephalosporins and aminoglycosides prevalence in clinicalisolates using beta regression models. None of the tested individual predictors were superior across all four investigated classes of antibiotics. For modelling of aminopenicillin resistance, a clearly higher Rvalue was obtained when isolate-based and gene-based data was combined as predictors, also after adjusting for the number of included variables. We conclude that there could be a value of including both isolate- and gene-based sewage data for predictions of resistance rates in clinical isolates, while emphasizing the value of linking predictors to specific species and classes of antibiotics.

title: Clonal diversity, virulence factors and antibiotic resistance genes of Enterococcus faecalis and Klebsiella pneumoniae from urban rats in Malaysia
abstract: Peridomestic rats serve as important carriers of zoonotic pathogens, including multidrug-resistant bacteria such asand. However, information on the clonal diversity, antibiotic resistance, and virulence of these pathogens in wild urban rats remains limited, particularly in tropical settings. This study investigatedandin urban rats from wet markets across four Malaysian states. A total of 277 rats (, = 177;, = 100) were trapped, and lung tissues were processed for bacterial isolation. Isolates were identified by 16S rDNA sequencing and examined for antibiotic susceptibility, resistance genes, and virulence factors using PCR. Clonal relationships were determined through multilocus sequence typing (MLST). Nineteenand sevenisolates were recovered. Allisolates carried multiple virulence factors (,,, and), and four tetracycline-resistant isolates possessed,, and. Five novelsequence types (ST730 - ST734) were identified. Allisolates carried the SHV gene; two also harbored FOX, and two possessedandvirulence factors. Two novelSTs (ST2641 and ST2642) were detected. Phylogenetic analyses revealed that both species displayed diverse sequence types scattered across global lineages. These findings suggest that urban rats may act as potential carriers of virulent and antibiotic-resistantand. These findings support the inclusion of urban rats in future One Health surveillance programs investigating antimicrobial resistance and virulent bacterial pathogens.

Copper-coated carbon nanotube surfaces for inhibiting biofilm formation by Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa
abstract: Biofilm-associated infections caused by clinically important pathogens such as() and() remain a major challenge in healthcare settings due to enhanced antimicrobial resistance and persistence. In recent years, copper-coated carbon nanotubes (Cu-CNTs) have gained considerable attention as promising antimicrobial nanomaterials for preventing biofilm formation on medical devices and hospital-associated surfaces. This review summarizes recent advances in the development and application of Cu-CNT-based antimicrobial coatings, with an emphasis on their antibacterial and antibiofilm activities against Gram-positive and Gram-negative pathogens. The synergistic combination of the high surface-area-to-volume ratio of CNTs and the potent antimicrobial properties of copper (Cu) ions enhances microbial inhibition. Previous studies suggest that Cu-CNTs interfere with initial bacterial adhesion, inhibit biofilm maturation, and disrupt established biofilms through mechanisms involving oxidative stress generation, membrane destabilization, and cellular damage. Furthermore, the review discusses the physicochemical characteristics, antimicrobial mechanisms, biomedical applications, and potential challenges associated with Cu-CNT coatings, including toxicity and biocompatibility concerns. Overall, Cu-CNT-based coatings represent a promising strategy for developing durable antimicrobial surfaces to control chronic biofilm-associated infections and reduce healthcare-associated contamination.

Harnessing hydrogel technology for advanced periodontitis therapy: A multifunctional approach to oral health restoration
abstract: Periodontitis is a bacterially driven inflammatory disease that can lead to tooth mobility and tooth loss. Conventional non-surgical therapy, antibiotics, and surgery may be limited by residual subgingival biofilms, antimicrobial resistance, and variable clinical outcomes. This review synthesizes recent studies of hydrogel-based systems for local periodontal therapy, focusing on stimuli-responsive release mechanisms, cargo-loading approaches, and regenerative outcomes in relevant animal models. Across these studies, hydrogels function as localized delivery matrices that can prolong retention at periodontal defects, regulate therapeutic exposure, and support tissue repair. We further evaluate translational considerations, including degradation behavior, long-termstability, and immunocompatibility. These findings position hydrogels as adaptable platforms for more precise periodontitis management and identify priorities for preclinical optimization before clinical translation.

title: Microbiota-constrained bacterial density limits phage infection in the gut and allows persistence of susceptible cells
abstract: With the rise of antibiotic resistance, bacteriophage-based treatments against bacterial infections have regained momentum. However, phage therapy has so far shown only moderate success in complex environments like the mammalian gut, where phages are particularly promising tools for microbiome engineering and specific elimination of opportunistic pathogens. Here, we use different murine models of intestinal colonization to quantitatively assess the minimal population size of susceptiblecells that is required for phage replication in the gut (replication threshold). We found that the composition of the intestinal microbiota is a key factor shaping phage-bacteria interactions by restricting the carrying capacity of susceptible host cells. We further demonstrate that the replication threshold enables coexistence of susceptible and resistant bacteria in phage-treated mice, with implications for phage-based applications in complex environments like the gut.

title: Values and trade-offs in responsible antibiotic behaviour and sustainable access: protocol for a comparative mixed-methods empirical ethics study in Sweden, Italy, and Bulgaria
abstract: Antibiotic resistance arises through biological evolution but is also shaped by behavioural, sociocultural, and institutional factors. Promoting responsible antibiotic behaviour requires understanding how members of the public and relevant stakeholders perceive antibiotic use, stewardship, access, and responsibility, and the values and trade-offs that shape their decisions. This study aims to investigate these factors across three national contexts and to develop context-sensitive recommendations and a methodological framework for future research. This protocol describes an ongoing comparative mixed-methods empirical ethics study conducted in Sweden, Italy, and Bulgaria from May 2025 to April 2028. The study comprises three connected components: semi-structured online interviews with 16-20 participants from four stakeholder groups in each country; a general-population survey incorporating a discrete choice experiment, with a minimum of 350 respondents per country; and iterative normative analysis using reflective equilibrium. The 3D Value Framework informs the interviews, which examine stakeholders' reasoning about sustainable antibiotic access, stewardship, responsibility, and preparedness. Interview findings, relevant literature, and previous research will inform the survey attributes and scenarios. The survey will examine public preferences and trade-offs concerning antibiotic treatment, responsible behaviour, and sustainable access, alongside antibiotic knowledge, trust, prosociality, biospherism, gender-related perspectives, social norms, and values. The empirical findings will be interpreted in relation to ethical theories of justice and personal and collective responsibility. A One Health perspective informs the overall study. By bringing stakeholder reasoning and public preferences into dialogue with normative analysis, the study will examine how responsibility for preserving antibiotic effectiveness and sustainable access should be understood and distributed between individuals and institutional actors. It will also address the ethical implications of trade-offs between present and future access and the distribution of associated benefits and burdens. This empirical ethics approach is expected to support a context-sensitive account of justice and responsibility and to inform ethically justified antibiotic stewardship, policy, and communication. Not applicable.

title: A sequence-informed hybrid framework for predicting antibiotic minimum inhibitory concentrations in previously unseen Escherichia coli pathogens
abstract: When an Escherichia coli pathogen is newly encountered, antimicrobial susceptibility information may be incomplete or unavailable. We investigated whether minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) could be predicted for previously unseen pathogens by jointly using pathogen genomic sequence information, antibiotic characteristics, and observed pathogen-antibiotic MIC patterns. The predictive value of integrating pathogen genomic information, antibiotic characteristics, and observed pathogen-antibiotic MIC patterns within a hybrid collaborative-filtering framework for previously unseen E. coli pathogens remains unclear. To develop and evaluate Model C for predicting MIC values in previously unseen, genomically characterised E. coli pathogens. The study used 9377 E. coli pathogens, 26 antibiotics, and 51,554 exact MIC measurements among 243,802 possible pathogen-antibiotic combinations. Model C combined observed MIC patterns, genomic features related to antimicrobial resistance (AMR), nucleotide-sequence comparisons across 265 AMR-related loci, and antibiotic characteristics. Five-fold pathogen-out validation excluded all MIC measurements from each test pathogen from training and model selection. The common validation cohort contained 9058 pathogens and 50,460 observed MIC values; Models 3B and 3 were evaluated as comparators. In pathogen-out validation of the 50,460 observed MIC values, Model C achieved a mean absolute error of 0.5931 log₂ MIC units, root mean squared error of 0.8477, and Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.9055. Model C performed best overall. A final model fitted to all 50,460 observed MICs predicted the remaining 185,048 unmeasured MICs. Model C estimated MIC values for previously unseen E. coli pathogens using genomic, antibiotic, and observed interaction information. Independent external validation is required. Predictions may help prioritise confirmatory testing but should not replace antimicrobial susceptibility testing or be used alone to guide treatment.

title: Emissions of quaternary ammonium compounds and pharmaceuticals from wastewater treatment plants under different operational conditions
abstract: The use of both quaternary ammonium compounds (QACs)-biocides increasingly consumed after the outbreak of covid-19-and pharmaceuticals causes concerns about adverse effects on aquatic organisms and links to antimicrobial resistance. Though they largely enter wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs), there exists a gap in knowledge of the effects of solids retention time (SRT) and hydraulic retention time (HRT) on their removal in the activated sludge process. We monitored 14 QACs, another disinfectant, and 13 pharmaceuticals in treated effluents of 14 activated sludge WWTPs with wide ranges of SRT (5-48 days) and HRT (7-70 h), within an administrative district over a year. The total mean concentrations of all compounds ranged from 2.4 to 15 μg/L among the WWTP effluents, to which 14 labile compounds (11 QACs and 3 drugs) contributed 6% to 76%. Their contributions were higher in WWTPs with shorter SRTs and HRTs. Relative standard deviations (RSDs) of effluent concentrations of labile compounds were mostly >50% among seasons and >100% among the WWTPs, largely exceeding those in raw sewage. The higher the WWTP removal rate of a compound was, the larger the effluent RSD was among the WWTPs and seasons. Per-capita mass outflows of most compounds other than persistent drugs were negatively correlated with SRTs or HRTs among the WWTPs, indicating that they were key factors affecting their removal and emission. Interpretation of these associations should consider the limited number of WWTPs and the availability of operational data. Our findings will be useful in managing QACs and pharmaceuticals.

title: Isolation, characterization, and therapeutic potential of a novel phage vB_KpiP_JZBo1 infecting Klebsiella pneumoniae
abstract: Klebsiella pneumoniae (K. pneumoniae) is an important opportunistic pathogenic bacterium that is often characterized by a multidrug-resistant phenotype, which can lead to the failure of antibiotic treatments. The emergence of multidrug-resistant K. pneumoniae, including carbapenem-resistant K. pneumoniae (CRKP), poses a significant threat to public health security. Bacteriophages, which are viruses capable of lysing bacteria, represent a promising alternative for treating infections caused by highly virulent K. pneumoniae and other antibiotic-resistant pathogens. In this study, we used K. pneumoniae 32b as the host bacterium and isolated the bacteriophage vB_KpiP_JZBo1. The optimal MOI of this bacteriophage is 0.01. And phage exhibited high activity across a wide range of temperatures (20°C - 50°C) and pH (4 - 11) following 1 h of incubation. Whole genome analysis revealed that the bacteriophage was a double-stranded DNA virus, encoding a total of 91 open reading frames (ORFs). Notably, genetic evolutionary analysis and BLASTN results indicated that phage vB_KpiP_JZBo1 shares the closest evolutionary relationship with K. pneumoniae phage KP8. However, genome-wide comparison revealed that they only exhibit 88% coverage and 93.03% nucleotide homology. This suggests that phage vB_KpiP_JZBo1 may be a novel species of phage. No genes associated with antibiotic resistance, virulence factors, and tRNA were found in the phage genome, and it belongs to Kaypoctavirus genus of the Schitoviridae family. Additionally, higher phage doses resulted in greater inhibitory and bactericidal effects against K. pneumoniae in LB medium. In model of G. mellonella, bacteriophage vB_KpiP_JZBo1 can effectively eliminate the infection of K. pneumoniae 32b and increase the survival rate of G. mellonella. These findings suggest that the bacteriophage vB_KpiP_JZBo1 has potential for the treatment and prevention of K. pneumoniae, and they also provide a theoretical basis for clinical applications.

title: Comparative effects and mechanisms of microbial inoculants and enzyme preparations on vermicomposting performance and antibiotic resistance reduction
abstract: Antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) in livestock manure pose risks to soil ecosystems and human health, yet their attenuation during vermicomposting remains incomplete even with earthworm activity. This study systematically evaluated whether two functional additive types, namely microbial inoculants and enzyme preparations, could enhance vermicompost conversion efficiency, compost quality, and ARG attenuation in cattle manure vermicomposting. Our results showed that most additives altered physicochemical properties and improved compost maturity, with the commercial compound microbial inoculant KM (trade name) achieving a germination index above 140%. Notably, acid protease treatment (VES) achieved a 27.5-percentage-point greater reduction in combined ARGs and integron-marker abundance than the unamended vermicomposting control (58.0% vs. 30.5%), indicating its potential for enhanced reduction of resistance-related abundance. Mechanistically, microbial inoculants (e.g., KM) effectively weakened ARG-integron marker-microbial co-occurrence associations through ecological network restructuring, whereas enzyme preparations (represented by acid protease) induced coordinated shifts in physicochemical properties and microbial community structure, which were associated with reduced ARG abundance. Additionally, spatial niche differentiation along the earthworm gut was associated with resistance-class-specific ARG distribution patterns. These findings indicate that microbial inoculants and enzyme preparations act through distinct ecological pathways in attenuating antibiotic resistance, providing a mechanistic basis for targeted additive selection in sustainable livestock manure valorization.

title: Could the next pandemic be fungal and could we respond effectively? From plausible pathways to operational preparedness
abstract: Fungal diseases cause substantial morbidity and mortality worldwide, yet they have been persistently neglected in pandemic preparedness plans, largely because no sustained human-to-human fungal pandemic has been documented to date. However, multidisciplinary evidence challenges the assumption that fungi are irrelevant to pandemic risk. Wildlife fungal pandemics show that mycoses can emerge on a global scale with catastrophic and irreversible consequences. Moreover, climate change is narrowing the mammalian thermal barrier against fungi, favouring heat-tolerant species, reshaping their global distribution, and thus facilitating zoonotic spillover. Rising human susceptibility-driven by ageing populations, immunomodulatory therapies, and increasingly complex health care-is intersecting with a substantial therapeutic gap, characterised by the absence of licensed vaccines, a limited range of antifungal agents, and increasing antimicrobial resistance. In this Personal View, we move beyond a synthesis of evidence to propose an operational framework for fungal pandemic preparedness, outlining plausible routes to pandemic-scale impact and the surveillance, diagnostic, therapeutic, One Health, and outbreak-response capacities needed to detect and contain emerging fungal threats before they become unmanageable.

title: Multi-Parameter In Vitro and Genomic Characterization of Bovine-Derived Bacteria with Probiotic Potential
abstract: Raw milk and bovine feces represent important sources of microorganisms with probiotic potential. This study aimed to identify potential probiotic candidates from bovine-derived samples and to comprehensively characterize their functional and safety-related features by integrating multi-parameter in vitro evaluation with whole-genome analysis. Acid-producing bacteria were isolated from 12 raw milk and 15 bovine fecal samples using bromocresol green agar. Following PCR-based exclusion of Escherichia coli and RAPD-PCR dereplication, the isolates were evaluated for acid and bile tolerance, survival under simulated gastrointestinal conditions, and autoaggregation, leading to the selection of five candidate strains: Lactiplantibacillus plantarum MX13, Lacticaseibacillus paracasei MX165, Enterococcus faecalis MX179, Enterococcus faecium MX125, and Enterococcus durans FX198. Further in vitro characterization revealed marked strain-specific differences in gastrointestinal stress tolerance, autoaggregation, cell-surface hydrophobicity, and antibacterial activity, with the two lactobacilli displaying broader antibacterial spectra than the Enterococcus strains. Multivariate analysis further revealed distinct overall phenotypic profiles among the candidates, with MX13 exhibiting a relatively balanced functional profile across the traits evaluated. Whole-genome analysis revealed clear differences between MX13 and MX125 in antimicrobial resistance-associated, putative virulence-associated, and other functional genomic features, providing additional information for candidate prioritization. Overall, this study identified and characterized five bovine-derived potential probiotic candidates with distinct functional properties through integrated phenotypic and genomic evaluation, providing a basis for their further functional validation and application-oriented assessment.

title: Histological disappearance of persistent clarithromycin-resistant Helicobacter pylori infection following administration of a sulforaphane-, curcumin- and Lactobacillus-containing food supplement: a case report
abstract: Increasing antimicrobial resistance has become a major challenge in the treatment of Helicobacter pylori infection. Sulforaphane, a bioactive isothiocyanate derived from broccoli sprouts, has demonstrated anti-H. pylori activity in experimental and clinical studies. Curcumin and probiotic bacteria have also been investigated as adjunctive therapies. A woman in her seventies underwent upper gastrointestinal endoscopy screening. Histology revealed chronic active Helicobacter pylori-associated gastritis involving the antrum and corpus. Molecular testing confirmed H. pylori infection and detected the clarithromycin resistance mutation A2143G in the 23S rRNA gene. Following treatment with bismuth quadruple therapy consisting of Pylera® (Laboratoires Juvise Pharmaceuticals, France: bismuth subcitrate potassium 140 mg, metronidazole 125 mg and tetracycline hydrochloride 125 mg per capsule; three capsules four times daily) plus pantoprazole (40 mg twice daily for 10 days, followed by pantoprazole 40 mg once daily for 4 weeks), repeat endoscopy 1 year later demonstrated persistent active gastritis and persistence of the resistance mutation. The patient subsequently received a nutraceutical preparation containing broccoli-derived sulforaphane, curcumin, and Lactobacillus acidophilus. The preparation was administered as two capsules twice daily before meals for 21 days. Follow-up endoscopy approximately 3 months later demonstrated resolution of inflammatory activity and the absence of detectable H. pylori organisms in antral and corpus biopsies. This case documents the histological disappearance of persistent clarithromycin-resistant H. pylori infection following administration of a sulforaphane-, curcumin- and probiotic-containing nutraceutical. Although causality cannot be established from a single observation, the findings support further investigation of such interventions in patients with treatment-refractory infection.

title: Exosome based nanocarriers enabling effective treatment of antimicrobial resistant infections through improved delivery and clinical potential
abstract: Exosome-mediated drug delivery recently emerged as a viable approach for enhancing the therapeutic effectiveness of antimicrobial medicines in combating multidrug-resistant (MDR) pathogenic bacteria. Due to their inherent biocompatibility, biomimetic membrane structure, and effective cargo transport abilities, exosomes confront numerous drawbacks linked to traditional antimicrobial delivery systems, such as suboptimal drug stability, restricted biofilm infiltration, insufficient intracellular delivery, and unintended toxicity. This analysis offers an extensive summary of the latest developments in exosome-facilitated antimicrobial delivery, emphasising the conveyance of antibiotics, antimicrobial peptides, nucleic acids, and hybrid nanotherapeutics. Processes through which exosomes increase antimicrobial effectiveness, such as improved biofilm infiltration, intracellular localisation, immune system modulation, and precise cargo delivery, are comprehensively discussed. Recent advancements in exosome manipulation, cargo-loading methodologies, hybrid exosome-centric systems, and pathogen-specific delivery techniques are critically reviewed. Furthermore, this review discusses critical translational obstacles including scalable production, cargo-loading efficacy, quality assurance, storage durability, regulatory harmonisation, and clinical application. The evidence gathered highlights the potential of exosome-based delivery systems as novel biomimetic nanocarriers in the battle against antimicrobial resistance. It also highlights the technological and regulatory developments required for their successful clinical application.

title: AI-enhanced biosensing for antimicrobial resistance: translating rapid diagnostics to global surveillance
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) necessitates rapid and reliable diagnostic technologies to support timely antimicrobial selection and stewardship. Although conventional culture-based antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) remains clinically important, its extended turnaround time limits timely intervention, while molecular diagnostics can rapidly identify resistance determinants but may not accurately predict phenotypic resistance. This review critically examines the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) with biomedical microdevices and biosensors for rapid AMR detection, encompassing microfluidic and lab-on-chip platforms, electrochemical and optical biosensors, and CRISPR-based technologies. Emphasis is placed on the application of AI for signal processing, noise reduction, pattern recognition, multiplexed detection, and predictive interpretation of complex biosensor outputs. Key translational challenges, including biofouling, matrix interference, sample-preparation variability, bubble formation, evaporation, signal drift, invalid-test rates, device reproducibility, and inadequate standardisation of reporting and validation, are critically evaluated. The requirements for embedded AI, including memory, computational resources, latency, and energy efficiency, are also considered for portable point-of-care deployment. Analytical, clinical, and operational validation are distinguished, with emphasis on prospective multicentre evaluation using representative specimens and reference AST methods. Beyond clinical diagnosis, AI-enabled microdevices offer potential for decentralised AMR surveillance across wastewater, agricultural, veterinary, and environmental settings within a One Health framework. Translation will require standardised datasets, generalisable and explainable AI, scalable manufacturing, regulatory oversight, data governance, and equitable deployment. Overall, AI-integrated biomedical microdevices represent a promising approach to rapid, decentralised, and actionable AMR diagnostics and surveillance, contingent on robust real-world validation.

title: Whole-genome characterization of a food-derived Kurthia gibsonii isolate reveals a tet(L)-str-repUS12 resistance-associated region
abstract: The emergence of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in environmental and food-associated bacteria has attracted increasing attention within the One Health framework. However, genomic information regarding antimicrobial resistance determinants and mobile genetic elements in Kurthia gibsonii remains limited. This study aimed to characterize a food-derived K. gibsonii isolate (KT09) by whole-genome sequencing, antimicrobial susceptibility testing, and comparative genomic analysis, with emphasis on the genetic context of a tet(L)-associated resistance region. (KT09), recovered from phyllo dough on gentamicin-supplemented medium was sequenced using Illumina platform. The reported draft genome consisted of 2,944,613 bp in 122 contigs > 500 bp (GC content, 36.65%; N50, 72,389 bp), with 99.34% completeness and 2.87% contamination by CheckM. TYGS analysis confirmed assignment to K. gibsonii. Disk diffusion showed variable inhibition-zone diameters, with particularly small zones for tetracycline and streptomycin. Genome analysis identified tet(L), str, and aadA1, while emrB was detected by genome annotation. The tet(L)-str-repUS12 resistance-associated region was located on contig00014, which showed a mean read depth of 290.97× and 100% breadth of coverage. Comparative BLASTn and synteny analyses showed high nucleotide similarity between this localized region and homologous chromosomal and plasmid-associated sequences from Kurthia, Enterococcus, and Staphylococcus. However, the complete contig was predominantly Kurthia-like and was not resolved as an independent circular component. The KT09 genome expands the limited genomic information available for food-derived K. gibsonii and documents a tet(L)-str-repUS12 resistance-associated region with close sequence similarity to plasmid-associated loci reported in other Gram-positive bacteria. These findings are consistent with a shared mobile gene pool but do not establish plasmid localization, mobility, or the source or direction of horizontal gene transfer. Long-read sequencing and experimental plasmid characterization are required to resolve the genomic location and transferability of this region.

title: From Destruction to Reconstruction: Substrate-Driven Biosynthesis of Antioxidants from Antibiotic Residues in Hyperthermophilic Composting
abstract: The accumulation of tetracycline (TC) in organic fertilizers poses severe risks by fostering antibiotic resistance in soil ecosystems. Hyperthermophilic composting effectively mitigates these threats, achieving nearly complete TC removal via thermal selection. Although previous studies have widely characterized the catabolic degradation routes of TC, we propose a novel transformation pathway in which TC-derived intermediates are redirected into secondary metabolism to synthesize antioxidant alkaloids and flavonoids. Integrated abiotic-biotic controls first demonstrated that while heat initiates breakdown, hyperthermophilic microbiota drive the subsequent deep transformation and diversification of products. FT-ICR-MS revealed that this process is underpinned by substrate restructuring, where recalcitrant compounds are depolymerized into bioenergetically favorable low-molecular-weight organic matter (LMW-OM). Cross-feeding assays confirmed that this accessible substrate pool significantly enhances cometabolic efficiency compared to conventional composting-derived substrates. Mechanistically, multiomics indicated that LMW-OM elevates intracellular NADH and ATP within the Thermus-dominated community, shifting metabolism from maintenance to active biosynthesis. Consequently, TC intermediates acting as structural mimics of endogenous aromatic precursors are recruited into these energized pathways to generate antioxidants.
