Crucially, diverting residues into anabolic networks eliminates the selective pressure exerted by intermediates, explaining the extensive attenuation of the antibiotic resistance genes. This work highlights pivotal substrate-microbe interplay, offering a new paradigm for converting antibiotic-laden waste into functional bio-organic fertilizers.

title: Peptidoglycan remodeling prevents antibiotic resistance during oxidative stress
abstract: The bacterial small RNA (sRNA) OxyS is expressed induring oxidative stress. The sRNA OxyS enhances cell survival by controlling genes involved in the regulation of hydrogen peroxide (HO) and iron-sulfur (Fe-S) cluster formation. Here, we used the MS2 affinity purification coupled with RNA sequencing (MAPS) technique to identify new target mRNAs of the sRNA OxyS. Our analysis revealed a significant enrichment ofmRNA, which encodes a peptidoglycan endopeptidase that promotes cell growth. Our results confirm a previous report on the sRNA OxyS repressing the translation of. We also found that an Δbackground facilitates the emergence of mutations, conferring increased resistance to the last-resort antibiotics polymyxin B and E (colistin), but only in the presence of the targetgene. This suggests that the translation repression ofby OxyS could prevent mutations in bacterial DNA during HO-induced oxidative stress. Moreover, we show that adding the antioxidant thiourea or sequestering iron in the Δbackground effectively reduces the emergence of resistance against both polymyxin B and colistin. These results suggest that reactive oxygen species (ROS), in conjunction with intracellular iron, play a key role in driving the emergence of antibiotic resistance. Overall, our work underlines a mechanism of antimicrobial emergence implicating oxidative stress, intracellular Fe, and cell wall remodeling in.IMPORTANCEThis study uncovers an underexplored link between peptidoglycan remodeling and oxidative stress responses during exposure to antibiotics. By elucidating how MepS and the sRNA OxyS interact in the presence of polymyxins and oxidative stress, our study suggests that MepS may exert an anti-mutator function. The repression oftranslation by OxyS seems to limit the emergence of antibiotic resistance driven by DNA mutations. Together, these findings suggest cell wall remodeling and oxidative stress response pathways as promising targets to enhance antibiotic efficacy and limit the emergence of resistance.

title: Temporal Trends and Associations of Antimicrobial Use and Resistance in Enterococcus Species From Broiler Farms in Canada
authors: van den Bergh J et al.
abstract: Antimicrobials are widely used in animal production for the treatment, prevention, and control of infectious diseases. However, antimicrobial use (AMU) is also a key driver of antimicrobial resistance (AMR). In response, the Canadian poultry sector implemented a phased three-step AMU reduction strategy to mitigate the emergence and spread of AMR. Enterococci are ubiquitous inhabitants of the gastrointestinal tract of animals and serve as important sentinel organisms for AMR surveillance because of their capacity to acquire AMR. This study investigated associations between farm management practices, including AMU, and AMR in enterococci isolated from broiler chickens. Farm management data were collected using standardized questionnaires, and faecal samples were obtained during farm visits. Phenotypic AMR profiles were determined by minimum inhibitory concentration testing of 623 isolates from 419 flocks across five Canadian provinces over a 4-year period. Generalized linear mixed models were used to evaluate associations between AMR and other factors, including AMU, province, year, breed, stocking density, downtime between flocks, and sanitation practices. Avilamycin use was significantly associated with avilamycin resistance in both E. faecalis and E. faecium. Provincial and temporal differences in resistance were observed for certain antimicrobials, with a notable decline in resistant isolates to Veterinary Drugs Directorate's Category II and III antimicrobials following implementation of the three-step AMU reduction strategy. These findings suggest that targeted AMU reduction strategies were associated with reducing AMR percentages in enterococci from Canadian broilers.

title: Genomic rearrangement of the capsule operon in a phylogenetically distinct cluster of the multi-drug-resistant Escherichia coli lineage ST131
abstract: ST131 is a dominant cause of multi-drug-resistant extraintestinal infections in humans. The lineage has a three-clade phylogenetic structure, of which clade C has gained resistance to multiple classes of antibiotics and is globally disseminated. As well as antimicrobial resistance, a number of virulence factors contribute to the success of ST131 clade C, including the production of capsule. Previous work on a limited number of strains has shown that the capsule operon in ST131 is highly variable. In this study, we analyzed the capsule genetics ofST131 by interrogating 3,033 genomes. Our data show a clonal distribution of capsule types and identify a monophyletic group of ST131 clade C strains that are characterized by an atypical capsule operon with highly divergent alleles of the keyandgenes. Our analysis suggests there is ongoing evolution within clade C of ST131, which looks to be driven not by the continuing evolution of antimicrobial resistance but by host-pathogen interactions.IMPORTANCEMulti-drug-resistant (MDR)is a problematic cause of invasive disease in humans and animals. Resistance to multiple classes of antibiotics is severely limiting treatment options. ST131-C is a highly successful, MDR clone ofthat is a major cause of extraintestinal infections. Capsule is a key virulence factor in contributing to this clone's success, with capsule switching allowing the bacteria flexibility to thrive in different niches. We present evidence that suggests continual evolution of this proliferant clone influenced by host-pathogen interaction. Small genetic changes can define the success of a clone; therefore, it is important to monitor this continual evolution in pathogens.

title: Enterobacteriaceae and Bacteriophages: Implications Against Antimicrobial Resistance
abstract: Enterobacteriaceae represent a clinically challenging bacterial family owing to the global emergence of multidrug resistance. Bacteriophages, the natural predators of these bacteria, have emerged as powerful tools for detecting, targeting, and inhibiting these pathogens. This review provides a comprehensive overview of bacteriophages targeting Enterobacteriaceae hosts, focusing on their diversity, virion architecture, and the molecular determinants of host specificity. The dynamic co-evolution between bacterial defence strategies and phage counter-defences is discussed to illustrate the complexity of the phage-Enterobacteriaceae host interactions. Translational applications of Enterobacteriaceae phages, including phage therapy, engineered phages, phage-derived lysins as antimicrobials, and phage-based diagnostics for rapid and specific pathogen detection is also explored alongside their limitations including limited large-scale clinical trials, regulatory and manufacturing hurdles, and the need for robust host-range prediction and standardization. Overall, this review elaborates implications of bacteriophage-Enterobacteriaceae interactions to combat antimicrobial resistance and support the development of next-generation antibacterial therapies and diagnostics.

title: Understanding Host-Phage Interactions in Chronic Wounds, Emphasising Inflammatory Markers and Neutralising Antibody Responses
abstract: BackgroundChronic wounds cause considerable morbidity, which is further compounded by antimicrobial resistance and biofilm formation. Bacteriophage therapy (BT) presents a promising alternative. However, issues such as host immune neutralisation and inflammatory reactions remain unresolved.MethodsThis prospective, interventional, non-randomized control study was conducted at the Institute of Medical Sciences, Banaras Hindu University, from July 2022 to February 2026. It involved 100 patients with chronic wounds (>6 weeks). It had two groups: Group I (n = 50) received bacteriophage therapy (BT), while Group II (n = 50) received conventional therapy (CT). Bacteriophages were isolated and applied topically every other day. Serum levels of IL-1β, IL-6, MMP-9, and TGF-β were measured using ELISA at baseline, immediately after therapy, and at six weeks after treatment completion. Neutralising antibodies in the BT group were measured through serum-phage interaction assays and data analysis was done.ResultsFollow-up was completed in 90% of patients. Diabetes (50%) was the most common comorbidity. The most commonly isolated bacteria were(30%),(26%), and(26%). The therapy duration was significantly shorter ( < .001) in the BT group (1.46 ± 0.63 months) than in the CT group (2.92 ± 1.02 months). Levels of IL-1β, IL-6, MMP-9, and TGF-β decreased significantly in both groups during and after treatment. Neutralising antibodies were detected in only 2 out of 45 BT patients (4.4%) with complete follow-up.ConclusionBT promoted faster wound healing without notably altering cytokine profiles. The fact that around 4.4% of patients developed neutralising antibodies, which did not interfere with healing, suggests that phage therapy can be safely applied.

title: Are Higher-Order Carbapenems Effective Therapy for Patients with Ertapenem-Resistant Enterobacterales Invasive Infections?
abstract: The IDSA guidance suggests treating Enterobacterales resistant to ertapenem but susceptible to imipenem or meropenem with a susceptible carbapenem in the absence of carbapenemase production; however, clinical outcomes data are limited. We conducted a multicenter prospective cohort study of hospitalized patients with invasive ceftriaxone-resistant Enterobacterales infections, comparing 30-day mortality between ertapenem-susceptible (ETP-S) and ertapenem-resistant (ETP-R) isolates. ETP-S isolates with an ESBL/AmpC phenotype served as the comparator because carbapenems are reliably active against these organisms. Carbapenem susceptibility was confirmed by broth microdilution. Inclusion criteria included: (1) susceptibility to imipenem or meropenem, (2) absence of carbapenemase genes, and (3) >72 hours of definitive therapy with imipenem or meropenem. Inverse probability weighting (IPW) adjusted for baseline differences, and logistic regression estimated odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals. Among 374 patients, 238 (64%) were infected with ETP-S and 136 (36%) ETP-R isolates. Baseline characteristics were balanced after IPW. ETP-R infection was associated with higher 30-day mortality (OR 2.24, 95% CI 1.26-3.98, p=0.006). Similarly, 14-day and in-hospital mortality were significantly higher among patients with ETP-R infections. The highest mortality was observed among patients with isolates resistant to two carbapenems (e.g., ertapenem and meropenem). Genomic analyses demonstrated enrichment of porin alterations and more non-carbapenemase β-lactamase genes (e.g., blaCTX-M, blaOXA-10) in ETP-R isolates. Among patients with Enterobacterales bacteremia treated with imipenem or meropenem, ETP-R isolates were associated with higher mortality than ETP-S isolates, challenging current guidance. This likely reflects combined porin loss and increased β-lactamase activity, potentially resulting in partial hydrolysis of higher-order carbapenems despite in vitro susceptibility.

title: Predictors of Antibiotic Overuse in Febrile Children: A Sub-analysis of the Prospective, Multicenter AutoPilot-Dx Study
abstract: Antibiotic overuse contributes to antimicrobial resistance. Mechanisms that drive overuse, including diagnostic uncertainty, are thought to be complex. We aimed to investigate predictive factors for antibiotic overuse in a large pediatric cohort. This is a subanalysis from the AutoPilot-Dx study, which enrolled febrile children 90 days to 18 years old presenting to the pediatric emergency department with respiratory tract infection or fever without source, including both hospitalized children and those discharged home. We analyzed patient flow from being treated with antibiotics at recruitment to definitive antibiotic treatment after assessment, depending on physician judgment. Variables significantly associated with antibiotic overuse in univariate analysis were entered into a multivariable logistic regression model to identify independent predictors of antibiotic overuse, defined as receipt of antibiotic treatment following clinical assessment in cases with viral panel-adjudicated diagnosis. Diagnostic uncertainty was assessed by treating physicians. Upon recruitment, 127/1008 (12.6%) were receiving antibiotic treatment. Overall, 186 of 628 cases with a viral panel-adjudicated diagnosis were judged to have antibiotic overuse. Factors with significant association in univariate analysis were diagnostic uncertainty, nonexudative tonsillitis, rales and younger age. Presence of a diagnostic test result upon presentation to the hospital and current antibiotic treatment were found not to be associated with overuse. Among 566 of 1008 cases with complete data on all model covariates, multivariable logistic regression yielded diagnostic uncertainty [odds ratio (OR), 2.09; 95% confidence interval (CI): 1.18-3.93; P = 0.015], nonexudative tonsillitis (OR, 2.78; 95% CI: 1.72-4.59; P < 0.001) and rales (OR, 1.82; 95% CI: 1.15-2.86; P = 0.01) to be positively associated with antibiotic overuse, while age showed a negative association in complete-case analysis (OR, 0.93; 95% CI: 0.85-0.99; P = 0.038), which attenuated and was no longer significant in a multiple imputation sensitivity analysis (OR, 0.96; 95% CI: 0.91-1.01; P = 0.150). Diagnostic uncertainty contributes to antibiotic overuse, alongside clinical factors. Future studies should investigate the impact of improved diagnostic algorithms on antibiotic prescribing in patients with respiratory tract infections in whom physicians experience diagnostic uncertainty.

title: The role, challenges, and innovations of rifampin in the management of periprosthetic joint infections: a narrative review
abstract: Periprosthetic joint infection (PJI) remains a severe complication due to persistent bacterial biofilms. Rifampin is traditionally valued for its unique biofilm-penetrating properties, yet its clinical role is increasingly viewed as context-dependent. While current evidence supports the efficacy of rifampin in two-stage revision arthroplasty, its application in debridement, antibiotics, and implant retention (DAIR) remains a subject of ongoing debate. Landmark randomized trials once reported superior cure rates for DAIR combined with rifampin, but contemporary large-scale retrospective data show no statistically significant difference in remission rates, often accompanied by a significantly higher incidence of adverse events. Furthermore, the timing of administration is critical; early initiation within five days post-DAIR has been linked to increased treatment failure. These challenges, alongside profound drug-drug interactions, have spurred interest in localized delivery innovations like microencapsulation and nanoparticles. While these bioengineering approaches show preclinical promise in overcoming PMMA chemical incompatibility, they remain at the proof-of-concept stage. Consequently, rifampin should be employed as a targeted adjunct rather than a universal standard, requiring careful consideration of surgical strategy, patient tolerance, and optimal timing.

title: Carbonaceous nanomaterials for the removal of hazardous pharmaceutical contaminants from wastewater: mechanisms, recent advances, and future directions
abstract: Rising pharmaceutical consumption and the continuous discharge of pharmaceutically active compounds (PhACs) into aquatic systems have become defining environmental challenges of the present decade. Because conventional wastewater treatment plants were never designed to remove biologically persistent micropollutants, trace residues accumulate in surface water, groundwater and drinking water, where they drive ecotoxicity, endocrine disruption and the dissemination of antibiotic-resistance genes. Therefore, understanding how nanomaterials can not only capture but also destroy these contaminants is central to safeguarding water quality. This review critically examines carbonaceous nanomaterials, such as graphene oxide, reduced graphene oxide, carbon nanotubes, graphitic carbon nitride, carbon dots and biochar, for PhAC removal, organised around the four dominant treatment routes: adsorption, membrane filtration, advanced oxidation processes (AOPs) and photocatalysis, the latter treated here as a light-driven hazard-oriented framework that achieves true mineralisation rather than the mere transfer of contaminants to another phase. The best-performing systems for the removal of representative drug classes, such as antibiotics, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, antidepressants, β-blockers and analgesics, are shown to share a common design motif: a conductive, defect-rich and often heteroatom-doped carbon scaffold that concentrates the pollutant, shuttles photogenerated charge carriers and stabilises a redox or light-active phase. Adsorption and membrane filtration routes deliver high capacity but relocate contaminants to a solid or concentrated phase, while carbon-coupled AOPs and S-/Z-scheme heterojunctions achieve contaminant degradation with concurrent antibiotic-resistance-gene reduction. Beyond removal efficiency, this review highlights catalyst stability, regeneration, reusability, total organic carbon (TOC) removal, transformation-product toxicity, energy demand, and performance in real wastewater matrices as critical parameters governing practical applicability. Finally, this review identifies key research gaps and emphasises the need for standardised, hazard-oriented assessment frameworks that integrate degradation efficiency, mineralisation, transformation-product toxicity, and environmental sustainability. Such an approach is essential for advancing carbonaceous nanomaterials from promising laboratory-scale technologies toward reliable and environmentally safe strategies for pharmaceutical-contaminated water remediation.

title: Antimicrobial resistance patterns in bacterial isolates from mice and rats in Australian laboratory rodent facilities between 2015 and 2024
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a critical global challenge threatening human and animal health, food security and economic stability. Despite advances in understanding AMR trends of bacteria from humans, domestic animals, wildlife and environmental sources, there is limited understanding regarding AMR profiles of bacteria isolated from laboratory animals, particularly rodents. To address this, a 10-year dataset from an Australian research animal health testing laboratory was analysed, investigating antimicrobial susceptibility patterns in bacterial isolates from laboratory mice and rats. Data from 205 isolates were reviewed, comparing AMR profiles across microbial species. Organisms undergoing antimicrobial sensitivity testing were most commonly associated with disease investigations, rather than routine health screening. In descending order, the most frequently isolated bacteria were Rodentibacter pneumotropicus, Staphylococcus xylosus, Enterococcus spp., E. faecalis, Enterobacter cloacae, Escherichia coli, Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella oxytoca and Proteus mirabilis. All isolates exhibited some AMR. Significant multidrug resistance (MDR) - with resistance to at least three of the following: tetracycline, trimethoprim-sulphamethoxazole, amoxicillin-clavulanic acid or ampicillin, or enrofloxacin - was observed in 22.0% of isolates. AMR was greatest in isolates from rats. Some MDR isolates included zoonotic bacteria, highlighting potential occupational health risks for humans and a risk of treatment failure in humans and laboratory rodents. Resistance patterns for R. pneumotropicus, E. faecalis and S. aureus were compared with those reported in similar studies from other regions, with greater rates of AMR observed in Australian isolates. Quantitative analysis was limited by small sample sizes; however, the data suggest further investigation and antimicrobial stewardship initiatives are urgently required.

title: A Biomimetic Microneedle Platform Using Neutrophil Membrane for Synergistic Antibacterial Therapy of MRSA Infection
abstract: Persistent bacterial infection has become life-threatening challenge worldwide. Bacterial biofilm formation, causing induced antimicrobial resistance and suppressive immune microenvironment, is one of the critical pathways leading chronic and persistent infection. Herein, an integrated microneedle patch harboring neutrophil membrane and antibiotics is designed to elicit therapeutic in-situ immunization for the management of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus infection. When applied on the infected skin, microneedles can physically penetrate the biofilm barrier, helping the diffusion of antibiotics to kill the bacteria deep in the biofilm. After breaking the integrated structure of biofilm, neutrophil membrane tightly binds to the bacterial debris to enhance the phagocytosis of antigen-presenting cells followed by the robust activation of T helper cells. Naïve B cells then differentiate to plasma cells or memory B cells to produce specific antibodies, thereby efficiently managing infection and preventing relapse. Overall, our study highlights the capability of eliciting therapeutic in-situ immunization mediated by the integrated biomimetic microneedle, providing an attractive perspective for the treatment of persistent bacterial infection.

title: Carbapenem resistance in pediatric Acinetobacter baumannii urinary tract infections: molecular determinants
abstract: In the pediatric population, carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii (CRAB) is a significant cause of hospital-acquired infections, particularly hospital-acquired urinary tract infections (HA-UTIs). There are a few studies on the molecular mechanisms of resistance to CRAB among children. To detect the prevalence of CRAB among children with HA-UTIs and to evaluate associated carbapenemase genes and clinical risk factors. This cross-sectional study included 100 children with HA-UTIs. Isolates were identified using standard microbiology techniques, and antimicrobial resistance (AMR) was detected according to the Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI) guidelines. Carbapenemase genes (blaOXA-23-like, blaOXA-24/40-like, blaOXA-58-like, and blaNDM) were detected by PCR. Data were statistically analyzed to assess the association between clinical factors and carbapenem resistance (CR). CR was identified in 73% of isolates. High rates of AMR were observed for cephalosporins and fluoroquinolones. The most prevalent gene was the blaOXA-23-like gene (60%), followed by the blaOXA-58-like (34%), the blaOXA-24/40-like (30%), and the blaNDM (15%). A significant association was observed between resistance to carbapenems and the carbapenemase genes blaOXA-23-like and blaNDM (p < 0.05). Clinical factors like ICU admission and catheterization did not show a significant association with resistance. Carbapenem resistance among pediatric Acinetobacter baumannii UTIs is highly prevalent and primarily driven by molecular mechanisms, particularly OXA-23 and NDM carbapenemases. This underscores the significance of molecular diagnostics and infection control in pediatric healthcare settings.

title: The weight of memory: nutrition, diabetes, and the brain
abstract: This issue of the Biomedical Journal explores therapeutic approaches to neuroinflammation, antimicrobial resistance, and cancer, as well as developments in laboratory testing and prognostic assessment. Experimental findings show that glibenclamide attenuates palmitic acid-induced hippocampal inflammation and memory impairment in mice. In antimicrobial research, CRISPR-Cas9-mediated elimination of resistance genes restores ertapenem susceptibility in resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae isolates, while deep learning offers an approach to interpreting antimicrobial susceptibility tests from images. Oncology articles span molecular characterization, treatment, and prognosis: BK polyomavirus integration and aristolochic acid exposure are associated with distinct molecular features in kidney transplant-associated urothelial carcinomas; bavachinin enhances cisplatin's antitumor activity in oral cancer models; biomarker changes inform prognosis during radium-223 therapy; and external validation supports the MAGIC-D model in advanced biliary tract cancer. Furthermore, research on cartilage homeostasis examines exercise-dependent responses of Prg4-expressing cells. Correspondence addresses combined radiotherapy and systemic treatment for hepatocellular carcinoma and, in a second exchange, stewardship of short-term systemic corticosteroid use.

title: Azelaic Acid as a Novel Antivirulence Agent Against Pseudomonas aeruginosa: In silico, In vitro and In vivo Efficacy and Biocompatibility
abstract: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is an opportunistic pathogen whose virulence is largely regulated by quorum sensing (QS), making this system an attractive target for anti-virulence therapies. Azelaic acid (AzA), a naturally occurring dicarboxylic acid widely used in dermatology, has not previously been investigated as a QS inhibitor. This study evaluated the antibacterial and anti-virulence activities of AzA against reference strains and multidrug-resistant clinical isolates of P. aeruginosa, together with its preliminary safety profile and potential molecular interactions with key QS proteins. Minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) ranged from 250 to 1000 μg/mL. At sub-inhibitory concentrations, AzA significantly reduced the production of pyocyanin, elastase, protease and alginate in a dose-dependent manner without affecting bacterial viability. Molecular docking predicted favorable interactions of AzA with LasI, LasR, PqsD and PqsR, supporting a potential modulation of QS-associated pathways. Chemoinformatic analyses predicted favorable drug-likeness and safety characteristics, while cell viability remained above 90% and hemolysis below 4% within the anti-virulence concentration range. In the Tenebrio molitor infection model, AzA significantly increased larval survival and reduced in vivo pyocyanin production in both the reference strain Pa14 and a multidrug-resistant clinical isolate. Collectively, these findings provide the first evidence that AzA can attenuates QS-regulated virulence in P. aeruginosa through complementary in vitro, in silico and in vivo approaches while exhibiting a favorable preliminary safety profile. These results support the repositioning of AzA as a promising anti-virulence candidate for the development of adjunctive therapeutic strategies against multidrug-resistant P. aeruginosa infections.

title: Fractionation of Terminalia mantaly stem bark extract enhanced antimicrobial, antibiofilm, and antioxidant activities: In vitro and multi-target in silico evaluation
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance remains a significant global threat, leading to a high mortality rate and the need for alternative treatments. This study aimed to determine the antimicrobial and antioxidant properties of liquid-liquid fractions from Terminalia mantaly stem bark extract and to investigate their potential multi-target interactions using in silico approaches. DPPH, ABTS, and FRAP assays, and cytotoxicity on Vero cells, were performed. The most active fractions were further evaluated for time-kill kinetics, antibiofilm activities, scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry profiling, followed by molecular docking, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, quantum-chemical calculations, and pharmacokinetics and toxicity profiling. Five fractions (F1-F5) showed minimum inhibitory concentrations ranging from 62.5 to 1000 μg/mL. Staphylococcus aureus ATCC43300 and Candida albicans ATCC14516 were the most susceptible strains, with F4 and F5 showing the highest activity against bacteria and F1 and F3 against yeast. The highest antioxidant activity was obtained with F1 against DPPH (ICof 237.4 μg/mL), F4 against FRAP (ICof 22.69 μg/mL), and F5 against ABTS radicals (ICof 23.46 μg/mL). SEM analysis indicated that the fractions disrupted the membrane and caused lysis of S. aureus. LC-MS profiling revealed 26 metabolites, with CNP0326236 and 6DTA identified as leads against AgrA, CrtM, and SarA. These findings suggest that modulation of quorum sensing, virulence factor expression, and cellular integrity may contribute to the observed antibacterial activity; however, these proposed mechanisms require experimental validation. Further studies, including mechanistic investigations and in vivo validation, are necessary to establish the antimicrobial potential of the identified lead compounds.

title: Can AI Help Repurpose Drugs to Fight Against Antibiotic Resistance?
abstract: Drug repurposing and development to meet the threat of antimicrobial resistance can be costly and time-consuming, but AI models may be able to help. In thisarticle, JMIR Correspondent Sara Novak reports on recent research training models to identify candidate drugs to treat resistant infections.

title: Phthalocyanine photosensitizers in antimicrobial photodynamic therapy as a multifunctional strategy for combating antimicrobial resistance
abstract: With antimicrobial resistance (AMR) on the rise, there is an urgent need for non-antibiotic approaches to treatment. Antimicrobial photodynamic therapy (aPDT) is being investigated as a non-antibiotic strategy for treating infections caused by multidrug-resistant (MDR) organisms. In this review we offer a thorough examination of phthalocyanines (Pcs) and metallophthalocyanines (MPcs), second-generation photosensitizers investigated mainly for bacterial and fungal photoinactivation. Antiviral aPDT is discussed separately because Pc-specific antiviral evidence remains comparatively limited. Our analysis focuses on how central-metal electronic configuration, spin-orbit coupling, and peripheral substitution influence intersystem crossing, triplet-state formation, and reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation in metallophthalocyanines. We also consider the physicochemical constraints that come with these compounds, namely their tendency to undergo aggregation-induced quenching (AIQ) in aqueous solution. To counter this and to get past the outer membrane of Gram-negative species, we evaluate synthetic changes such as cationic peripheral functionalization. The paper further explores how Pcs are being combined with pharmaceutical nanotechnology - be it liposomes, metallic nanoparticles or graphene oxide - to improve bioavailability and open the door to synergistic photothermal therapy (PTT). The promise of Pc-conjugates linked to bioactive agents like antibiotics is likewise noted. Yet for all the in vitro and preclinical data accumulated over the years, phthalocyanine-based aPDT has seen little use in the clinic. We close with an appraisal of the reasons for this shortfall, from issues of dosimetry and localized hypoxia to difficulties in penetrating biofilms, and put forward the case for engineering stimulus-responsive nanoplatforms as a way to bridge the regulatory and biological divide.

title: Parental knowledge, antibiotic-seeking behavior, and inappropriate antibiotic use in children with respiratory tract infections: a narrative review of behavioral drivers and implications for antimicrobial resistance
abstract: Inappropriate antibiotic use is one of the main modifiable drivers of antimicrobial resistance (AMR). Children with respiratory tract infections receive a large share of avoidable prescriptions, and the reasons lie as much in behavior, communication, and access as in clinical need. To synthesize evidence on the clinical, prescriber-related, parental, communication-related, access-related, and socioeconomic drivers of inappropriate antibiotic use in children with respiratory tract infections, and to appraise the evidence for interventions that target these drivers. We conducted a narrative review guided by the SANRA criteria. PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science, supplemented by Google Scholar, were searched for English-language peer-reviewed studies published between January 2014 and December 2025. Thirty studies formed the core thematic synthesis. A supplementary search identified trials and reviews used to appraise stewardship interventions. In countries like Italy and Finland, there was a significant decrease in pediatric prescriptions for uncomplicated respiratory infections, despite not being any increase in the occurrence of serious complications. Similarly, studies on acute otitis media indicated low benefits but abundant side effects. Although the parents were often misinformed about this process, knowledge alone was not sufficient to guarantee proper practice. Numerous studies revealed that physicians estimated the parents' needs incorrectly, and numerous children ended up receiving antibiotics that were not even asked for by their parents. One of the reasons for this issue was that patients were purchasing non-prescription medications, using leftover antibiotics, and limiting their access to affordable medical care. Research showed that communication, auditing, and clinical decision support training helped in reducing antibiotic prescriptions, while national training programs were not able to provide similar successes. The inappropriate utilization of antibiotics among children is a result of influences from different levels: household, consultations, pharmacy and health system levels. These factors should be treated as associations instead of identified causes due to the fact that the majority of the evidence provided is cross-sectional. There is some evidence suggesting that a combination of clinician-targeted strategies with dispensing and access for medications is more promising than just education alone.

title: Zidebactam as a new approved β-Lactamase inhibitor with intrinsic antibacterial activity via PBP2 binding
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance continues to challenge the clinical efficacy of established antibiotics, highlighting the need for innovative therapeutic strategies. Cefepime/zidebactam combines a fourth-generation cephalosporin with a novel diazabicyclooctane β-lactamase inhibitor endowed with intrinsic PBP2-targeting activity. This commentary discusses the pharmacology, mechanism of action, and medicinal chemistry of zidebactam, focusing on its distinctive peculiarities. Complementary PBP2/PBP3 targeting, together with serine β-lactamase inhibition, provides a multifaceted strategy to restore and enhance β-lactam activity against resistant pathogens. The chemical structure highlights two key functional groups: an acyl-hydrazide-derived side chain ending in a piperidine ring, which enables recognition of PBP2, and a DBO nucleus containing a urea group that reacts with the active site serine residue in beta-lactamases.

title: Comparative antimicrobial potential of silver and zinc oxide nanoparticles versus chlorhexidine and tetracycline-based local drug delivery agents against periodontal pathogens: a systematic review
abstract: The objective of this study is to compare the antimicrobial effectiveness of Silver (Ag) and Zinc oxide (ZnO) nanoparticles with both Chlorhexidine and Tetracycline used as TDS's through in-vitro studies.The study employed a systematic review following the PRISMA guidelines to identify and select studies published up to 2025 from the electronic databases PubMed, Scopus, Cochrane, and WEB of Science. No search limit was set. Studies selected reported in vitro comparisons between Ag and/or ZnO nanomaterials and traditional antimicrobial drugs using oral microbial pathogens. Both assessors independently performed study selection, data extraction, and quality assessment using the Joanna Briggs Institute checklist. The primary outcomes were minimum inhibitory concentrations and zones of inhibition. Of the ten studies included in this analysis, none of the studies found Ag nanoparticles to be less effective than chlorhexidine against a range of microorganisms; however, Ag nanoparticles had significantly lower minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) values than chlorhexidine and had a significantly larger zone of inhibition than chlorhexidine in most studies examined. Zinc oxide nanoparticles were found to have moderate, concentration-dependent antimicrobial activity, which tended to be comparable to chlorhexidine, but not to antibiotic tetracycline. Ag nanoparticle-antibiotic combinations exhibited a synergistic effect in seven of the studies reviewed. Few studies reported a risk of bias. Based on the included in vitro studies, Ag nanomaterials demonstrated promising direct antimicrobial activity against periodontal pathogens. However, owing to methodological heterogeneity and the absence of clinical evidence, definitive conclusions regarding their superiority or routine clinical use cannot yet be drawn. Further standardized biological, preclinical, and clinical investigations are warranted.

title: A substrate-dependent mechanism of inhibition of the polyspecific multidrug efflux pump MexF from Pseudomonas aeruginosa
abstract: presents a significant challenge in both clinical and antibiotic discovery settings due to the low permeability of its cell envelope. Efflux pumps acting synergistically with the permeability barrier of the outer membrane provide efficient protection against various antibacterial agents. Among 12efflux pumps from the resistance-nodulation-division (RND) superfamily, the MexEF-OprN efflux system-and its transporter component MexF-remains relatively underexplored. MexEF-OprN is not expressed under laboratory conditions but plays an important role duringinfections as well as in clinical antibiotic resistance, particularly against fluoroquinolones and trimethoprim. To gain mechanistic insights into MexF functions, we identified and characterized SLU-1642, a small-molecule inhibitor featuring a 2-aminobenzothiazole core that selectively targets MexF and its closest homologs, but not major efflux pumps such as MexB with overlapping substrate specificities. Using a combination of experimental and computational approaches, we found that SLU-1642 specifically potentiates the activity of antibiotic substrates of MexF inhyperporinated strains overexpressing MexF. Our results indicate that small chemical modifications of SLU-1642 modulate efflux inhibition in a substrate-specific manner. Furthermore, only some of the substrates, such as doxycycline, but not trimethoprim, are sensitive to the SLU-1642 action against MexF variants, with amino acid substitutions changing the transport efficiency of the pump. Taken together, our findings establish SLU-1642 as a MexF-selective efflux inhibitor with a mechanism of action dependent on the potentiated substrate.

title: Functional export of NDM-7 to outer membrane vesicles in Klebsiella pneumoniae compromises imipenem and cefiderocol activity
abstract: The carbapenemasescarbapenemase (KPC) and New Delhi metallo-β-lactamase (NDM) are the most widespread determinants of carbapenem resistance in. Whereas KPC is a soluble periplasmic serine-β-lactamase, NDM is a membrane-anchored metallo-β-lactamase (MBL), a feature that promotes its incorporation into outer membrane vesicles (OMVs). OMVs are naturally released nanoparticles that deliver diverse bioactive cargo, including enzymes, virulence factors, and signaling molecules, and may contribute to antibiotic resistance. Here, we investigated the export and activity of carbapenemases in OMVs produced by carbapenem-resistantclinical isolates expressing NDM-7, an emerging NDM variant, or KPC-2, as well as in isogenic laboratory-derivedstrains producing NDM-1, NDM-7, or KPC-2. NDM enzymes were detected in vesicles released by NDM-producing strains, whereas KPC-2 was detected in whole-cell lysates but not observed in purified OMVs. OMVs contained catalytically active NDM enzyme and conferred protection to susceptibleagainst imipenem. Importantly, NDM-positive OMVs also promoted the survival of susceptible bacteria during exposure to cefiderocol, a siderophore cephalosporin used to treat infections caused by MBL producers, allowing the recipient strain to grow at otherwise inhibitory concentrations. This protective effect was more pronounced for NDM-7 than for NDM-1. Together, these findings show that the clinically emerging NDM-7 variant is efficiently packaged into OMVs inand remains enzymatically active, allowing extracellular antibiotic degradation and conferring protection to susceptible bacteria exposed to carbapenems and cefiderocol.

title: Engineering Hybrid Peptides and Ionic Liquid-Peptide Conjugates for a Fast Action on Bacterial Membranes
abstract: Fast-acting peptide-based antimicrobials that target bacterial membranes are herein addressed and promise a breakthrough in chronic wound care. Two peptide hybrids (3.1-PP4 and PP4-3.1), engineered by us, resulted from linking PP4 (a non-antimicrobial anti-aging peptide used in cosmetics) to the antimicrobial peptide 3.1. In contrast, the replacement of the latter with an antimicrobial ionic liquid afforded an ionic liquid-peptide conjugate C16-Im-PP4. Herein, we demonstrate their rapid bactericidal action by targeting bacterial membranes via a combination of biophysical assays and microscopy using liposome models of bacterial membranes and live bacteria. Interestingly, the peptide hybrids share a similar membrane-disruptive mechanism against Gram-positive Staphylococcus aureus and Gram-negative Escherichia coli. In turn, the ionic liquid-peptide conjugate C16-Im-PP4 displayed bacterial-type-dependent behavior. These findings underscore the potential of peptide-based agents to address chronic wounds, which remain vulnerable to infection due to prolonged inflammation and rising antibiotic resistance that is increasingly regarded as a "silent pandemic".

title: Synergistic antibiotic activity and integrated genomic-metabolomic profiling of patch- and plaque-derived Staphylococcus aureus in mycosis fungoides
abstract: Mycosis fungoides (MF), the most common form of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, is frequently associated with skin dysbiosis, and advanced lesions are often dominated by multidrug-resistant. To characterize microbiologically relevant properties of MF-associated, we evaluated synergistic antibiotic combinations and performed integrated phenotypic, genomic, and metabolomic profiling. Several antibiotic combinations, most notably carbenicillin combined with either gentamicin or levofloxacin, exhibited pronounced synergistic activity and restoredantimicrobial activity against highly resistant isolates. Comparative genomic analyses revealed substantial variability between isolates in resistomes and virulence repertoires, including enterotoxins, immune-evasion, and stress-response factors. Metabolomic profiling further revealed isolate-specific extracellular signatures, including putrescine and urocanic acid. In summary, this study identifies promising antibiotic combinations against multidrug-resistantstrains. Furthermore, this exploratory investigation demonstrates phenotypic and genomic heterogeneity among MF-associatedisolates, warranting further evaluation in larger longitudinal studies. Despite its predominance in advanced mycosis fungoides (MF) lesions, the role of multidrug‑resistantin adverse clinical outcomes remains poorly understood. Bridging the gap between clinical observations and microbiological mechanisms is essential to clarify howpersists in MF skin and to identify therapeutic alternatives for‑positive patients, for whom treatment options remain limited. This study addresses two major clinical needs: the lack of effective antibiotic strategies and the limited understanding of bacterial factors that may contribute to worsened clinical outcomes. By integrating synergistic antibiotic testing with genomic, phenotypic, and metabolomic profiling, our work highlights clinically relevant heterogeneity among MF-associatedisolates. These findings identify promising therapeutic directions and establish a framework for future large-scale longitudinal studies to better understand the role of diversestrains in MF pathogenesis.

title: Activity of omadacycline and comparator agents against rapidly growing mycobacteria by broth microdilution and whole genome sequencing
authors: Calado Nogueira de Moura V et al.
abstract: Pulmonary infections caused by rapidly growing mycobacteria (RGM), such as, are challenging to treat, highlighting the need for new therapeutic options. This study evaluated theactivity of omadacycline against RGM and investigated the influence of tetracycline resistance mechanisms on itsactivity.susceptibility to omadacycline and comparator antimicrobials was assessed by broth microdilution against 476 geographically diverse RGM isolates from the United States. Omadacycline minimal inhibitory concentration (MIC) distributions were compared between cystic fibrosis (CF) and non-CF RGM isolates. Variation in the TetR-TetX operon and the,, and(41) genes was evaluated by whole genome sequencing. Omadacycline exhibited low MIC values across all RGM species (MIC/MIC: 0.25/0.5 µg/mL). CF isolates showed a modest shift toward higher omadacycline MIC values (= 0.001). The activity of comparator antimicrobials varied by species, whereas omadacycline was consistent and comparable to tigecycline. The TetR-TetX operon was present in all sequenced isolates, with variable amino acid sequences across species. These variations did not significantly affect omadacycline or tigecycline activity, whereas doxycycline and minocycline remained largely inactive regardless of TetR-TetX variation. TheA1408G mutation was identified in 6% ofisolates, andmutations were identified in 4% of isolates. The T28C(41) sequevar was present in 80% ofsubsp.and 100% ofsubsp., whereas 100% ofsubsp.exhibited a truncated(41). Omadacycline consistently demonstrated potentactivity across RGM species regardless of TetR-TetX operon variation, supporting its potential role in treating RGM infections. Rapidly growing mycobacteria (RGM) are a group of bacteria that often resist common antibiotics, making the infections they cause hard to treat. In this study, we tested omadacycline, a newer antibiotic in the tetracycline class, against a large collection of these bacteria collected from patients across the United States. We found that omadacycline showed consistent activity against different RGM species, requiring low concentrations to inhibit bacterial growth in laboratory testing. These findings support further evaluation of omadacycline as a potential treatment option for patients with RGM infections, which can be challenging to manage.

title: A Comparative Study between Escalation and De-escalation of Antibiotics in a Tertiary Care Hospital: A Prospective Observational Study
abstract: Antibiotic de-escalation is a key component of antimicrobial stewardship that aims to optimize antimicrobial therapy while reducing the emergence of antimicrobial resistance, treatment-related adverse events, and healthcare costs. However, evidence regarding its implementation in emergency care settings in India remains limited. This study evaluated the clinical characteristics and antibiotic utilization patterns among patients managed with antibiotic de-escalation versus escalation in a tertiary care hospital. This prospective observational study was conducted over 18 months in the Emergency Department of Indira Gandhi Institute of Medical Sciences, Patna, India. A total of 200 adult patients receiving empirical antibiotic therapy were enrolled. Patients were classified into de-escalation (n = 140) or escalation (n = 60) groups based on clinical response and predefined criteria assessed within 48 h of admission. Demographic characteristics, sequential organ failure assessment (SOFA) score, acute physiology and chronic health evaluation II (APACHE II) score, laboratory parameters, and antibiotic prescribing patterns were analyzed. Continuous variables were compared using Student's t-test or Mann-Whitney U-test, and categorical variables using the Chi-square or Fisher's exact test. P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Of the 200 enrolled patients, 70.0% underwent antibiotic de-escalation and 30.0% required escalation. At admission, significant differences were observed between the groups in total leukocyte count (TLC) (P < 0.001), liver function test values (P = 0.006), blood urea nitrogen (BUN) (P < 0.001), and serum creatinine (CREAT) (P = 0.002), whereas SOFA and APACHE II scores were comparable. After 48 h, significant differences were observed in SOFA score (P = 0.004), TLC (P < 0.001), BUN (P < 0.001), and serum CREAT (P < 0.001). Carbapenems and β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitor combinations were the most frequently prescribed empirical antibiotics. Antibiotic utilization patterns differed significantly between the two groups, with patients in the de-escalation group more frequently receiving combination antibiotic therapy (P < 0.001). Clinical and laboratory parameters improved significantly following de-escalation during the first 48 h. Antibiotic de-escalation was feasible in most patients admitted to the emergency department and was associated with favorable early clinical and laboratory outcomes. These findings support the incorporation of de-escalation strategies into antimicrobial stewardship programs to promote rational antibiotic use. Larger multicenter studies are warranted to evaluate the impact of antibiotic de-escalation on mortality, antimicrobial resistance, and long-term clinical outcomes.

title: The Genetic Legacy of Thermal Processing in Pasteurized Foods: Persistence of Antimicrobial Resistance Genes, Potential for Horizontal Gene Transfer, and a Proposed Genetic Legacy Index
abstract: Thermal processing inactivates foodborne bacteria but does not necessarily destroy their DNA, membrane vesicles, or bacteriophage particles. Such residues persist in pasteurized milk and heat-treated meat and are ingested by consumers. Whether this material can transfer antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs) to gut bacteria remains untested: the only direct human evidence of foodborne resistance-gene transfer involved live bacteria, not material released from heat-killed cells. This narrative review synthesizes evidence on the post-thermal fate of extracellular DNA, membrane vesicles, and bacteriophages, grading that evidence explicitly from detection of a target sequence, through structural integrity, to demonstrated transfer under realistic conditions. Persistence of ARG sequences after pasteurization is well documented, whereas functional transfer from foodborne dead-cell material has not been demonstrated. A Genetic Legacy Index (GLI) is proposed as a conceptual measurement framework-not a validated index-combining extracellular DNA abundance, ARG load, and ARG-mobile genetic element linkage, with an illustrative formula, normalization strategy, and validation agenda. Current finished-product microbiological criteria are predominantly culture-based and do not establish limits for extracellular or dead-cell genetic material, although integrated antimicrobial resistance surveillance increasingly includes molecular detection and whole-genome sequencing. The GLI is therefore proposed as a research and surveillance tool rather than a product-release criterion: a first step toward evaluating an unquantified exposure pathway within One Health surveillance of the food chain.

title: Interfacial Polymerization Using Acyl Chloride-Functionalized Porphyrin Comonomers toward Robust PA-66 with Type I/II Dual Photodynamic Antibacterial Durability
abstract: The growing threat of bacterial contamination and antibiotic resistance urgently requires functional antibacterial textiles. Photodynamic antibacterial approaches relying on reactive oxygen species (ROS) provide a promising alternative to achieve safe and long-term antimicrobial protection. Herein, a fabrication strategy was developed to construct intrinsically photodynamic antibacterial polyamide 66 (PA-66) yarns via interfacial polymerization. Acyl chloride-modified porphyrin (TCPP-Cl4), acting as a ternary monomer, was covalently grafted onto PA-66 molecular chains via interfacial polymerization. Subsequent drawing, spinning, and twisting yielded functional TCPP-Cl4-PA-66 yarns that preserved the favorable mechanical performance and thermal stability of PA-66. Physically blended TCPP/PA-66 yarns were also prepared as reference samples. Compared with TCPP/PA-66 yarns, the covalent anchoring process effectively reduced photosensitizer leaching and improved ROS generation capacity. As a result, TCPP-Cl4-PA-66 yarns achieved antibacterial efficiencies of 97.4 ± 1.3% against Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus) and 94.0 ± 2.8% against Escherichia coli (E. coli). Furthermore, this covalent immobilization also endowed the yarns with favorable washing resistance, maintaining stable photodynamic antibacterial activity against both strains after multiple washing cycles. Interwoven fabrics fabricated from TCPP/PA-66, TCPP-Cl4-PA-66, and cotton yarns also exhibited desirable photodynamic antibacterial performance. This work provides a facile strategy for constructing photodynamic antibacterial textile materials with good stability.

title: Surgical Site Infection and Antimicrobial Resistance After Mastectomy in Dogs and Cats: A 615-Case Multicentre Cohort and Infection-Control Audit
abstract: Surgical site infection (SSI) is an important complication after mastectomy and antimicrobial resistance may complicate treatment. To estimate 30-day SSI incidence after mastectomy in dogs (Canis lupus familiaris Linnaeus, 1758) and cats (Felis catus Linnaeus, 1758), evaluate patient- and procedure-related factors, describe perioperative antimicrobial use and microbiology and assess clinic infection-control practices. This multicentre retrospective cohort included 615 mastectomy procedures from 12 veterinary clinics in Tehran Province, Iran, between 2020 and 2025. SSI-positive records were independently re-reviewed by two investigators using contemporary veterinary SSI terminology. Clinic-stratified conditional logistic regression evaluated seven clinically selected predictors. SSI occurred after 54/615 procedures (8.8%; 95% CI, 6.8%-11.3%); 50 infections were superficial and four deep. Surgical duration per 30 min (aOR, 2.37; 95% CI, 1.61-3.49), intraoperative hypothermia (aOR, 3.66; 95% CI, 1.39-9.62), body condition score per point (aOR, 1.60; 95% CI, 1.05-2.42) and previous major surgery (aOR, 3.57; 95% CI, 1.49-8.55) were associated with SSI. An MDR isolate was identified in 16/33 cultured SSI cases and antimicrobial-isolate discordance was present in 15/30 assessable comparisons. Mean clinic infection-control audit score was 4.6 ± 1.7/10. Longer surgery, intraoperative hypothermia, higher body condition score and previous major surgery were associated with SSI in this predominantly canine cohort of intact animals undergoing mastectomy without concurrent ovariohysterectomy. These associations were not independently demonstrated in cats. The findings support standardised surveillance, perioperative risk reduction, culture-guided treatment and antimicrobial stewardship. Not applicable. This was a retrospective observational study and clinic-level audit and was not a clinical trial.

title: What Is the Evidence for Silver Resistance in Chronic Wounds? A Systematic Review of Prevalence and In Vitro Studies
abstract: Silver-containing wound dressings are among the most widely used topical antimicrobial interventions in chronic wound management. Amid escalating antimicrobial resistance and increasing scrutiny of antiseptic stewardship, there is growing debate regarding the prevalence and clinical relevance of bacterial resistance to silver, yet the available evidence has not previously been systematically evaluated with a specific focus on chronic wound populations. This review aimed to evaluate the published evidence on the prevalence of silver resistance in bacteria isolated from chronic wounds and to summarise experimental evidence on the capacity of wound-associated isolates to acquire reduced silver susceptibility in vitro. We searched MEDLINE, Embase and Scopus in accordance with PRISMA guidelines, identifying 2190 records, of which five publications met eligibility criteria. Two publications investigating overlapping isolates were consolidated, yielding four independent datasets. Three prevalence datasets reported markedly different rates: studies from the United Kingdom and Sweden identified low phenotypic resistance (0 of 112 and 1 of 56 isolates) and sil gene prevalence (< 2% in both), while a study from Bangladesh reported substantially higher phenotypic resistance (31.5%) and sil carriage (30.9%). Regional differences in antibiotic use offer a plausible explanation but were not directly tested in any included study and concordance between genotypic and phenotypic resistance was poor throughout. Two in vitro induction studies produced divergent results by endpoint: reduced planktonic susceptibility reverted towards baseline once silver exposure was withdrawn, whereas substantial increases in biofilm eradication concentration in Pseudomonas aeruginosa persisted. Prevalence was low where examined, but three datasets from three countries cannot establish the global burden of silver resistance in chronic wounds and critical gaps remain in geographic representation, methodological standardisation and validated breakpoints. Current evidence is insufficient to support changes to guidelines or policy in either direction.

title: Impetigo Antibiotic Stewardship and the Need for Treatment Alternatives
abstract: Impetigo is a highly contagious bacterial skin infection, primarily caused by Staphylococcus aureus and, less frequently, Streptococcus pyogenes. Although typically self-limiting, treatment is recommended to reduce symptom burden, limit transmission, and prevent complications. Increasing antimicrobial resistance to commonly used topical antibiotics presents a growing challenge, highlighting the need to develop new topical antibiotics and incorporate antibiotic stewardship principles into impetigo management. A structured literature review was conducted to evaluate the clinical efficacy, safety, and antimicrobial resistance associated with topical treatments for impetigo. An international panel of dermatologists, including pediatric dermatologists and a pediatrician, convened in February 2026 to review the evidence and provide clinical insights on stewardship-informed management strategies. Topical antibiotics remain first-line therapy for localized uncomplicated impetigo. However, resistance to topical antibiotics commonly used to treat impetigo (eg, mupirocin, fusidic acid, and retapamulin) has been widely reported. Antibiotic stewardship is an essential component of impetigo management and promotes the use of the right antibiotic for the right duration. Topical ozenoxacin, which acts against organisms resistant to other topical agents and has a low capacity for developing resistance, may help address existing gaps and support stewardship-informed care. Impetigo represents an important opportunity for antimicrobial stewardship in dermatology. Consideration of local trends in antibiotic resistance, antibiotic-sparing strategies, and use of novel agents may help optimize management and address current limitations in care.

title: Awareness and Prescribing Practices for Doxycycline Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (doxyPEP) Among Healthcare Providers Delivering Sexual Health Care in Australia: A Cross-Sectional Survey
abstract: We surveyed 215 healthcare providers delivering sexual health care in Australia about doxycycline post-exposure prophylaxis (doxyPEP) for sexually transmitted infection prevention. Awareness was high (190/215, 88.4%) and half of those aware (94/190, 49.5%) had prescribed doxyPEP in the past 6 months. Among those who had not prescribed doxyPEP in the past 6 months, concern about antimicrobial resistance was the most frequently reported reason (85/121, 70.2%).

title: Molecular and metabolic features of colistin-resistant ST11 carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae
abstract: The emergence of colistin-resistant carbapenem-resistant(CRKP) poses a critical threat to public health, a challenge that was exacerbated by the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic.The specific metabolic adaptations that underlie colistin resistance in high-risk sequence type 11 (ST11) CRKP clinical strains, particularly in direct comparison with their susceptible counterparts, remain poorly characterized.To explore metabolic features associated with colistin resistance in clinical CRKP isolates.Twelve CRKP strains, encompassing both colistin-resistant and colistin-susceptible isolates, were analysed for antimicrobial resistance profiles, virulence-associated genes, sequence types and biofilm formation capacity. Comparative untargeted metabolomics was performed to map metabolic shifts between the resistant and susceptible groups.All isolates belonged to the high-risk clone ST11, harboured the KPC-2 carbapenemase and carried multiple virulence genes, with K2 being the dominant serotype. All isolates formed biofilms, with resistant isolates showing enhanced capacity. Colistin resistance was chromosomally mediated byandmutations, with no plasmid-encodedgenes detected. Untargeted metabolomics identified 126 significantly differentially expressed metabolites (DEMs) between resistant and susceptible isolates. These DEMs were significantly enriched in lipids and lipid-like molecules. Colistin-resistant strains exhibited increased glycerophospholipids, sphingolipids and fatty acids, coupled with decreased metabolites from central carbon and amino acid pathways.In this exploratory study, colistin resistance in these ST11 CRKP strains was associated with chromosomal alterations inandand with marked shifts in membrane-associated lipid metabolites. While these metabolic changes suggested membrane remodelling, they remain associative and require functional validation. Beyond resistance, the co-carriage of these traits with robust virulence gene expression highlights a critical clinical challenge, supporting the need for further research into combination therapies targeting these adaptive lipid pathways.

title: Benchmarking nanopore-based strategies for antimicrobial resistance prediction
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) presents a pressing need to ensure that the right antimicrobials are used to target the right microbes at the right time. Ideally, the appropriate antimicrobial is selected after patient samples have been cultured and assessed with antimicrobial sensitivity testing (AST). However, the time needed for culture-based diagnosis leads to immediate empirical treatment, often with broad-spectrum and/or high-tier antimicrobials. Direct nanopore metagenomic whole-genome sequencing to identify pathogens and predict their AMR is a rapid and patient-side alternative. A limitation of this approach is potential inconsistencies in i predicted AMR phenotypes. Here, we benchmarked the current performance ofAMR prediction strategies for nanopore-generated long-read data. Using real-world nanopore data paired with AST phenotyping for 201 samples representing 27 bacterial species, we assessed the impact of basecalling mode, data volume and assembly strategy and compared the performance of eightAMR prediction tools with seven AMR databases. We found that basecalling accuracy mode does not significantly affect the overall accuracy ofAMR predictions but assembly strategy and data volume both do. Prediction tools using the ResFinder database scored best for balanced accuracy (0.80±0.02 for both ResFinder and ABRicate), whilst DeepARG scored best for sensitivity (0.65±0.03); predictions were more accurate for some antibiotic classes and genera than others. However, even the best-performingAMR prediction strategy missed some resistance identified by lab-based AST. We conclude, therefore, that currentlyAMR prediction can supplement lab-based AST but cannot yet replace it.

title: Risk Factors for Colonization With Antibiotic-Resistant Bacteria Among Hospitalized Patients in Bangladesh: An Antibiotic Resistance in Communities and Hospitals (ARCH) Study
abstract: Antibiotic-resistant bacteria (ARB) are frequently linked with healthcare settings, but specific factors associated with colonization within healthcare settings in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) remain poorly understood. This study explores risk factors for ARB colonization among hospitalized patients in Bangladesh, where 82% were colonized with extended-spectrum cephalosporin-resistant Enterobacterales (ESCrE), 37% with carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales (CRE), and 21% with methicillin-resistant(MRSA). Hospitalized adults from 3 hospitals in Dhaka completed interviews and underwent chart review to assess healthcare exposures. We used bivariate analyses, random forest variable selection, and multivariate logistic regression to identify factors associated with ESCrE, CRE, and MRSA colonization. ESCrE colonization was associated with admission to a non-medical ward (aOR 2.16-8.57, 95% CI 1.14, 64.4) and hospitalization ≥ 3 days before specimen collection (aOR 1.74, 95% CI 1.13, 2.69) while being inversely associated with age (≥45 years, aOR 0.54-0.58, 95% CI .29, .99) and carbapenem use (aOR 0.02, 95% CI < .01, .14). CRE colonization was associated with hospitalization ≥ 3 days before specimen collection (aOR 1.56, 95% CI 1.08, 2.23), third-generation cephalosporin use (aOR 2.93, 95% CI 2.02, 4.23), and other beta-lactam use (aOR 4.83, 95% CI 2.65, 8.81). MRSA colonization was inversely associated with third-generation cephalosporin use (OR 0.60, 95% CI .38, .95). Antibiotic use, duration of hospitalization, age, and ward type were associated with ARB colonization among hospitalized patients. Further investigations into antibiotic use patterns and infection prevention and control practices may identify modifiable risk factors to reduce ARB in healthcare settings in LMICs.

title: The Broad Ecological Range of Salmonella enterica Serotype Typhimurium Is Associated With Genomic Diversification
abstract: Salmonella Typhimurium is a versatile foodborne pathogen with a broad ecological range, making it an ideal model to better understand pathogen adaptations that allow them to infect multiple hosts and persist across environments. Here, we analysed 595 genomes of S. Typhimurium representing three food animal sources (bovine, swine, and poultry) and one non-food animal source (wild birds). We found that S. Typhimurium from food animal sources generally had a more open pangenome and harboured more antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs). Notably, swine isolates exhibited the most open pangenome and the highest prevalence of ARGs, patterns that were associated with a greater presence of mobile genetic elements, particularly plasmids. Despite similar core genome sizes, S. Typhimurium from different sources displayed distinct patterns of positive selection in the core genome that varied in frequency and targeted functional categories. In contrast, although accessory genome sizes varied substantially across sources, the frequency of positive selection remained similar. Using machine learning, we identified source-predictive genetic variants, many of which are associated with stress-response functions. These findings suggest that gain and loss of accessory genes and positive selection acting on core genes support differential adaptation in S. Typhimurium, potentially contributing to its broad ecological range.

title: Long-term impact of an antimicrobial stewardship programme on antimicrobial use and selected clinical outcomes: A 15-year interrupted time series study
abstract: To evaluate the long-term impact of an antimicrobial stewardship programme (ASP) based on prospective audit and feedback on antimicrobial use and selected clinical outcomes. We conducted a single-centre interrupted time series analysis evaluating antimicrobial use before (2008-2016) and after (2017-2023) implementation of an audit-and-feedback-based ASP. Consumption was expressed as defined-daily-doses per 100 occupied bed-days (DDD/100 OBD). The model included ASP implementation and COVID-19 onset in 2020. Trends were benchmarked against the VINCat surveillance network. Secondary analyses included incidence density of multidrug-resistant bloodstream-infections (BSI) and 14-day associated mortality, methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) and Clostridioides difficile infection (CDI). ASP implementation was associated with significant reductions in piperacillin/tazobactam consumption -1.40 DDD/100 OBD (95% CI -2.47 to -0.33) and a non-significant decrease in carbapenem use, accompanied by increased use of narrower-spectrum antipseudomonal cephalosporins. Although a sustained decrease in total antimicrobial use was not achieved, trends were more favourable than in VINCat hospitals (annual slope difference -0.64 DDD/100 OBD; 95% CI -1.21 to -0.065). No significant changes were observed in multidrug-resistant BSI incidence or 14-day mortality. MRSA incidence decline during the study period, while CDI incidence remained stable. This audit-and-feedback-based ASP was associated with sustained shifts towards narrower-spectrum antimicrobial use and more favourable consumption trends compared with peer hospitals. However, no significant reductions in overall antimicrobial use or key clinical outcomes were observed, highlighting the challenges of achieving measurable clinical impact in real-world hospital settings.

title: Antimicrobial resistance in Escherichia coli urinary isolates from primary care in Galicia (Spain), 2023-2024: Trends and relationship with antibiotic consumption
abstract: The objective of this study was to describe antimicrobial resistance patterns of Escherichia coli isolated from urine samples in primary care and to identify trends relevant to empirical treatment of urinary tract infections. We conducted an observational, retrospective, multicenter study including 49,746 E. coli isolates from urine samples obtained between January 2023 and December 2024 in ten hospital microbiology laboratories in Galicia, Spain. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing followed EUCAST guidelines. Resistance rates were analyzed by age, sex, and temporal trends. Outpatient antibiotic consumption data from the Galician Health Service (2015-2024) were reviewed to correlate associations with resistance patterns. E. coli was more frequently isolated in women, with higher rates in older adults. Resistance to amoxicillin-clavulanic acid increased compared with 2016-2017, whereas resistance to ciprofloxacin and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole declined. Fosfomycin resistance remained stable, and nitrofurantoin resistance appeared lower, likely reflecting updated breakpoints. Multidrug resistance was uncommon (3.37% for cefotaxime+ciprofloxacin+trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole; 1% for cefotaxime+ciprofloxacin+trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole+gentamicin). In two hospitals, ESBL-producing isolates showed significantly higher resistance to fosfomycin (p<0.001). Resistance was consistently higher in men and older. Trends in outpatient use of amoxicillin-clavulanic acid and ciprofloxacin partially mirrored resistance patterns. Fosfomycin and nitrofurantoin remain appropriate in vitro empirical options for E. coli acute uncomplicated cystitis in women managed in primary care. Rising amoxicillin-clavulanic acid resistance and the prevalence of ESBL-producing isolates underscore the need for targeted antimicrobial stewardship. Continuous surveillance is essential to guide empirical therapy and limit the emergence of multidrug resistance.

title: Mycobacterium abscessus bacteremia: A narrative literature review based on a case report
abstract: Mycobacterium abscessus is a highly virulent nontuberculous mycobacterial complex (NTM) that frequently exhibits high-level antimicrobial resistance. Bacteremia is uncommon and occurs predominantly in immunocompromised patients. We report a catheter-associated bloodstream infection by M. abscessus subsp. massiliense, and review M. abscessus bacteremia published over the past 10 years. A PubMed search was conducted from 1 January 2015 to 31 December 2025, using the terms "M. abscessus bacteremia" and "M. abscessus catheter infection and bacteremia". Clinical, microbiological, therapeutic, and outcome variables were analyzed. 22 episodes of M. abscessus bacteremia were documented (ours included). The most frequent sources were catheter related infections (8 cases), skin and soft-tissue infection (4), surgical procedures (4) and underlying pulmonary disease (3). 86% of patients had underlying conditions considered risk factors for infection. Overall mortality was 31.8%. Amikacin, macrolides, and carbapenems were the most commonly used agents, with prolonged treatment durations and frequent regimen modifications due to resistance or toxicity. M. abscessus bacteremia is rare event with a significant mortality. Rapid microbiological identification and early initiation of appropriate empiric therapy are critical to improving outcomes.

title: Genomic characterization of Clostridioides (Clostridium) difficile in Cambodia
abstract: Genomic studies can provide insights into genetic determinants of virulence, antimicrobial resistance (AMR) and transmission pathways of. Here, we characterized the core genome ofstrains belonging to the five most common ribotypes (RTs) found in Cambodia.Whole-genome sequencing was conducted on 48 toxigenicstrains belonging to RTs 017, 012, 046, 014/020 and 056, recovered in 3 previous epidemiological studies in Cambodia between 2022 and 2023. Toxin and AMR genes were detected, and MLST was determined. Comparative genomic analysis was conducted within strains isolated in Cambodia and between strains from Cambodia and Thailand.ST2/RT 014/020 was the most genetically diverse [14-2,563 core-genome SNPs (cgSNPs)], whilst ST37/RT 017 was the most clonal (0-32 cgSNPs). Clonal strains (defined as sharing ≤2 cgSNPs) were observed within ST34/RT 056, ST37/RT 017 and ST54/RT 012 groups. One strain of ST37/RT 017 from Cambodia differed by eight cgSNPs from a strain from Thailand isolated in 2018. Resistance geneswas the most prevalent, followed by,,,,,,,and. Genotypic multidrug resistance, genotype associated with the phenotype, was found in 100% of ST37/RT 017 strains and 67% of other strains.The transmission ofin Cambodia occurred not only among genetically distinct strains but also clonal strains. Besides sources within the country,could have also originated from neighbouring countries such as Thailand. A high number of AMR determinants in most strains indicates the necessity for strict AMR surveillance in the country.

title: Cefepime Dose Individualization in Early Sepsis: A Pragmatic Feasibility Trial Protocol
abstract: Cefepime is a core antibiotic in sepsis treatment, yet standard dosing yields 10- to 30-fold exposure variability in critical illness. In the early "golden hours" of sepsis, low cefepime levels (affecting up to 70% of cases) may lead to organ dysfunction progression, treatment failure, and antimicrobial resistance. Empiric dose escalation to overcome low levels can increase the risk of dose-dependent neurotoxicity. We developed and qualified a population pharmacokinetic model using patient weight and estimated glomerular filtration rate from creatinine and cystatin C that, in simulation, improved attainment of effective and safe drug levels. To describe the Beta-Lactam Optimization and Outcomes Management (BLOOM) 1 pragmatic feasibility trial. This single-center, cluster-randomized, pragmatic feasibility trial (ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT07287332) was approved with a waiver of informed consent. Participants are critically ill adults (age ≥ 18 yr), hospitalized at Mayo Clinic (Rochester, MN), who are receiving cefepime for suspected or documented sepsis. A screening tool embedded in the electronic health record (EHR) identifies eligible patients newly initiated on cefepime (≤ 1 previous dose in 48 hr) who are then randomized to care groups (clusters) that use an individualized dosing algorithm (intervention) or usual-care dosing (control). Exclusions are cephalosporin allergy, acute kidney injury, kidney replacement therapy, extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, and missing inputs required for the algorithm (weight, creatinine, cystatin C). Recruitment began on January 15, 2026, and is expected to conclude by January 2027 (target enrollment, ≥ 300 patients). For eligible patients, EHR-embedded clinical decision support prompts the cluster-assigned dosing approach, with final dose decisions made by the clinical team. Feasibility, fidelity, and exploratory pharmacokinetic and clinical outcomes will be assessed using mixed methods. This workflow-integrated pragmatic feasibility trial will determine whether personalized cefepime dosing can be implemented in routine practice to optimize timely sepsis therapy while maintaining safety.

title: Drug prescribing patterns among burn patients in a tertiary care teaching hospital in Assam, India: A prospective observational study
abstract: Burn injuries are a significant public health concern, particularly in developing countries, resulting in high morbidity, mortality, and healthcare burden. Management of burn patients requires integrative pharmacotherapy with multiple drugs, encompassing polypharmacy which necessitate inviting rational prescribing and antibiotic stewardship. To evaluate the prescribing patterns among burn inpatients in a tertiary medical college hospital and assess the compliance with essential medicines lists (EMLs). A prospective observational study was organized in the burn unit over 1 year (January-December 2023). Data on demographics, burn characteristics, including total body surface area (TBSA) estimation, and prescribed drugs for 109 admitted patients were recorded using a data collection form. Drug utilization patterns were analyzed using descriptive statistics. Adherence to the National List of Essential Medicines (NLEM) and the World Health Organization Essential Medicines List (WHO-EML) was estimated. The mean age of patients was 25.2 ± 16.3 years, with a male prevalence of 68.8%. Most burns were accidental (97.2%), with a mean TBSA of 28%. Polypharmacy pattern was observed with an average 6.8 numbers of drugs per prescription. Antibiotics, analgesics, gastroprotectives, and intravenous fluids were routinely prescribed. Cephalosporins (75.22%) and nitroimidazoles (70.64%) were the most frequently used antibiotic groups, with ceftriaxone being the most common. Paracetamol and tramadol were the most prescribed analgesics. Adherence to NLEM and WHO-EML was 100% and 90%, respectively. The study demonstrates extensive use of multiple drugs in burn management, with a predominance of empirical antibiotics.
